definitions.definition: The reflection of consciousness in the intellect, compared to the sky reflected in a pond; unreal, a product of ignorance; the jīva as agent (Rāma-hṛdaya, Rāma Gītā).

An appearance manifested by consciousness within itself as if external (ĪPK 1.5.1); the world is ābhāsa, real as manifestation; the individual too manifests (ābhāsana) as the first of his five acts (PH 11).
Semblance: the jīva as a mere appearance of consciousness in the intellect (Sureśvara); in BS 2.3.50 'reflection'.

notes: Contrasted by the tradition with Advaita's vivarta (see dsp:causation, dsp:world-real-or-appearance).

definitions.definition: A dependent reality of three kinds: prior non-existence, destruction and constant (absolute) non-existence; mutual non-existence (difference) is not a fourth, being the nature of things. Known by inference and by perception.
The seventh category, of four kinds (prior, posterior, absolute, mutual); not listed by Praśastapāda because determined through its counterpositive, not because unreal (Udayana).
Proposed as a means of knowledge (in the sense of non-apprehension); reduced to inference (NS 2.2.2).
Where the five positive means of knowledge do not arise, the non-apprehension itself is the means of knowing non-existence (ŚV abhāva 1; the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Not a separate means: the Prakaraṇapañcikā counts five means only; absence is grasped as the bare locus (as the Kāśikā on the Ślokavārttika reports the Prābhākara view).
The safety the renouncer gives to all beings on going forth (MDh 6.39–40).
Fearlessness: 'brahman is fearlessness' (BAU 4.4.25); Janaka has reached fearlessness (4.2.4); fear arises from a second (1.4.2); the knower of bliss is never afraid (TU 2.4, 2.9).
The renouncer's gift: 'fearlessness to all beings from me'.
Hostile sorcery; one class of Atharvavedic rites.
The first daily period: purification and approaching the Lord (going to the temple).

Words first express their own meanings and cease; the expressed meanings then connect to yield the sentence-meaning, as the flame is an intermediate stage in cooking with wood (Śabara on MS 1.1.25; ŚV vākya 342–343).
The nature of ahaṃkāra (SK 24); also the misidentification by which puruṣa seems colored (SS 6.28).
Clinging to life, flowing by its own momentum, present even in the wise (2.9); the wish 'may I not cease, may I be', a fear of death that shows former births (YBh 2.9).
Consecration conferring the office of teacher (ācāryābhiṣeka) or of power-seeker (sādhakābhiṣeka).
Bathing of the installed image; in Kerala, kalaśa-abhiṣeka rites renew the deity's power.
Production understood as the manifestation of what already exists, as a pot is manifested by a lamp (SS 5.59; cf. 1.120).
That which was covered by the void before That One was born by tapas (RV 10.129.3); its sense (life-force, emptiness, the germ) is debated by commentators.
Practice: effort toward the mind's stability (1.13), firmly grounded when long, uninterrupted and devoted (1.14); with dispassion the means of stilling (1.12).
Practice, which together with dispassion restrains the restless mind (BhG 6.35); a step of the devotional ladder (12.9).
Practice, with dispassion a support of meditation (SS 3.36) and of the cessation of coloring (SS 6.29).
Repetition of an injunction, which would be pointless unless it marks a distinct rite (MS 2.2.2); in Vedānta usage one of the six marks of purport.

notes: Mīmāṃsā sense; distinct from abhyāsa 'practice' in Yoga.

definitions.definition: Repeated practice of bringing the mind back to the Lord; the second step of the ladder of BhG 12.9, and the 'yoga of practice' of 8.8.
The first result of dharma (VS 1.1.2); sought through visible means where the visible result is absent, and through pure food with restraint (VS 6.1.8, 6.2.1, 6.2.9 C).
The practice of the good (sadācāra) as a source of dharma (MDh 2.6); without it the Vedas do not purify (VDh 6.3).
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the bhakta stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
The teacher who, initiating the student, bears him three nights as an embryo (AVŚ 11.5.3).
The true teacher (sadācārya) of the unbroken lineage, who imparts the five sacraments and the secret mantras out of compassion.
The teacher who initiates and teaches the Veda with its ritual and secret parts, 'from whom one gathers the dharmas' (ĀpDh 1.1.1.14); ten times more venerable than a sub-teacher (MDh 2.145).
Teacher: knowledge learned from a teacher leads most surely to the goal (ChU 4.9.3); 'a person who has a teacher knows' (ChU 6.14.2); 'let your teacher be a god to you' (TU 1.11.2).
The consecrated teacher (also deśika, guru) empowered to initiate and to perform installations.
Being held as one's own by a true teacher, which the Śrīvacanabhūṣaṇam teaches is itself sufficient for salvation for one who can do nothing else.
Consecration of an initiate as ācārya, entitled to initiate others and teach.
Insentient reality: eternal (the Vedas), eternal-and-non-eternal (Purāṇas etc., time, prakṛti), and non-eternal products, uncompounded and compounded.
Inconceivable: what cannot be established or refuted by reasoning and is known only from revelation — used of the Lord's powers.
Inconceivable simultaneous difference and non-difference of the Lord and his powers (souls, world); inconceivable because his powers are beyond reason.
Insentient reality in three kinds: pure sattva, mixed sattva (prakṛti) and that devoid of sattva (time); the body of the Lord together with the souls.
The non-conscious reality, of three kinds: aprākṛta, prākṛta and time.
Instruction, teaching formula: 'now the instruction: not so, not so' (BAU 2.3.6); the teaching about brahman in lightning and in the mind (Kena 4.4-5); the teaching of 'I' and of the self (ChU 7.25).
A support-point of attention in the body (sixteen in the Yogacūḍāmaṇi); the base centre.
The tāmasa opposite of virtue (SK 23), leading to downward movement (SK 44).
A quality of the self produced by forbidden acts (Tarkasaṅgraha).
What is made known by prohibition as leading to harm (anartha), e.g. the violence aimed at in the Śyena rite; also the demerit (pāpa) that results.
Suffering caused by humans, animals, birds, reptiles, insects and plants (commentaries on SK 1).
Perishable existence (BhG 8.4).
The Puruṣa (BhG 8.4).
With respect to the gods (the cosmos), paired with adhyātma (ChU 3.18; Kena 4.4).
Suffering from supernatural or cosmic agencies: cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning (Gauḍapāda) or possession by yakṣas, rākṣasas and planets (Vācaspati).

Eligibility for knowledge and scripture, in three grades (low, middle, highest) by birth and by qualities; the highest is the dispassionate renunciant devoted to Viṣṇu. Eligibility to Veda, Tantra or the Name is distinguished by class and gender.

The qualification of the agent entitled to perform a rite and enjoy its fruit: a human (MS 6.1.4–5), man or woman — husband and wife jointly (MS 6.1.8, 6.1.17) — of the three higher varṇas, with Vedic learning (MS 6.1.25–38); the subject of adhyāya 6.
An injunction that conveys ownership (enjoyership) of the fruit of the act, e.g. 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice'.
A topic-section of the sūtras treated in five steps: subject, doubt, prima facie view, conclusion and connection.
The unit of Mīmāṃsā discussion, with five members: subject, doubt, connection, prima facie view and conclusion (Nyāyamālā).
The eligible agent of a rite, the one to whom the fruit belongs ('one desiring heaven').
The qualified student: purified by prescribed duties and endowed with the four means.
The need for a controller, a proof of puruṣa (SK 17); in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, governance by mere proximity, like a magnet (SS 1.96).
Substratum: the real on which something unreal is superimposed (the rope for the snake; Brahman for the world).
The Lord himself in the body (BhG 8.4).
The three time-paths (past, present, future) in which properties stand; past and future exist in their own form because of this difference (4.12).
The six 'paths' of the cosmos — letters, words, mantras, kalās, principles and worlds — purified in nirvāṇa-dīkṣā.
The six paths - letters, mantras, words; kalās, tattvas, worlds - contemplated from gross to supreme (VBT 56-57; TĀ 6-12).

notes: Parallels the Sarvāstivāda term adhvan (see brw:sarvastivada-yoga-time-and-transformation).

definitions.definition: The priest who performs the ritual actions speaking the Yajus formulas.
Deliberate superimposition by scripture and teacher (creation, sheaths, attributes) as a provisional teaching device.

Superimposition: 'the appearance, of the nature of memory, of something previously seen in something else' — the mutual superimposition of self and not-self that is the basis of all empirical life, called avidyā.

Superimposition: the appearance of one thing as another through error, like a snake in a rope; ego is the first superimposition on the Self; jīva and witness appear mutually superimposed like fire and iron.
The own nature (svabhāva) of the Imperishable (BhG 8.3); the knowledge of the self is the best of sciences (10.32).
With respect to the self/body, as opposed to adhidaivata, with respect to the gods: the two registers in which the Upaniṣads state correspondences (ChU 3.18; Kena 4.4-5).
Inner clarity in the lucidity of nirvicārā coalescence (1.47): a clear light of insight grasping things as they are, without sequence (YBh 1.47).
The yoga of the inner self, by which the wise one realizes the hidden god and leaves joy and sorrow (KU 1.2.12).
Learned from the Yoga śāstra: austerity, breath-control, withdrawal, meditation, fixation (NBh 4.2.46).
Knowledge of the self as in the Upaniṣads; Nyāya is more than this because of its separate categories, though in it knowledge of truth is knowledge of the self (NBh 1.1.1).
Internal suffering, bodily (from imbalance of wind, bile and phlegm) and mental (from desire, anger, separation from the dear, etc.) (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati on SK 1).
The nature of buddhi (SK 23); perception is determination concerning each object (SK 5), explained by Vācaspati as a predominance of sattva in buddhi.
The accomplishment of gaining knowledge of the twenty-five principles by studying texts (SK 51; Gauḍapāda).
The hereditary Śaiva priests (Śivācāryas, gurukkaḷ) of South Indian temples, entitled to parārtha worship.
Mother of the Ādityas, before whom one prays to be sinless (RV 1.24.15); born of Dakṣa, and Dakṣa of her (10.72.4).
The sons of Aditi (Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman and others), who stand by ṛta (RV 10.85.1).
Kapila as the first knower who, assuming a created mind, taught the doctrine to Āsuri out of compassion (saying quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya on YS 1.25, ascribed to Pañcaśikha).
The unseen cause of motions without visible cause and of the mind's passage at death and birth; its absence is liberation (VS 5.1.15, 5.2.14, 5.2.19–20 C).
The residue of past action that brings about the body (NS 3.2.60); set in motion by the Lord (NBh 4.1.21).
Unseen force; used by Śāstradīpikā for what awakens impressions in dreams, and generally for the unseen results of acts, of which apūrva is the Mīmāṃsā form.

equivalents.note: Mīmāṃsā's apūrva is the unseen potency produced by a rite; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika's adṛṣṭa is merit/demerit as qualities of the self — both link act to later result.

literal: to be experienced in an unseen birth

definitions.definition: Karma ripening in a future life; none remains for one whose afflictions are exhausted (YBh 2.12).

Rejected as a practice for the worshipper at the māheśvara stage, since worship rests on difference (SSM 10.37–43), and affirmed at the aikya stage, where difference is seen to be imagined by māyā (14.8–14).
Without a second, non-dual: 'he becomes the ocean, the one seer without duality' (BAU 4.3.32); the fourth is 'peaceful, auspicious, non-dual' (MāU 7, 12).

notes: The adjective of the Upaniṣads; the school-name Advaita Vedānta is later.

definitions.definition: The inclination toward non-duality, which arises only by the grace of the Lord.
Faultless speech; above all the authorless Veda and the other true scriptures, the only means by which Viṣṇu is known.
Testimony: the activity arising in a hearer from the words of a reliable speaker who has seen or inferred the matter (YBh 1.7); it too reaches only the general (1.49).
The teaching that has come down through the succession of teachers from Maheśvara.

Revealed Śaiva scripture spoken by Śiva/Sadāśiva, the 'higher knowledge' as against the lower knowledge beginning with the Veda; in South Indian usage especially the 28 Siddhānta scriptures and their upāgamas.
The Pāñcarātra saṃhitās as scripture spoken by Bhagavān himself (Bhagavacchāstra).

notes: A widely quoted etymology (ā-gata from Śiva's mouth, gata to Girijā, mata by Vāsudeva) is of uncertain source and not recorded as a definition here.

definitions.definition: Karma done after knowledge, which does not cling to the knower, as water to a lotus leaf.
An offence, especially against the gods' ordinances, which the worshipper asks Varuṇa to loosen like a rope (RV 2.28.5).
Fire and the god of fire: household priest and messenger between men and gods, carrier of oblations, present in all fires, guardian of ṛta (RV 1.1).

The year-long building of the great brick fire-altar (often in the shape of a falcon) in five layers, explained in ŚB 6–10 as the rebuilding of Prajāpati who fell apart, so that the sacrificer builds and becomes an immortal self.

The twice-daily milk offering into the sacred fires by one who has set them up; the Brāhmaṇas explain it as healing the junction of day and night (ŚB 1.6.3.36), as an offering of 'truth in faith' when nothing else exists (ŚB 11.3.1.4), and as a cycle through the worlds and the body (ŚB 11.6.2).
Interiorized as the offering into the breaths at meals (ChU 5.19–24) and as the continuous 'inner Agnihotra' of speech and breath (KU 2.5).
Offerings into the consecrated fire in a kuṇḍa, part of daily and occasional worship.
The formless (amūrta) worship of Viṣṇu through fire offerings.
Devotion without motive and without interruption to the Supreme Person, flowing to him like the Gaṅgā to the sea (Kapila); also 'animittā'.
Devotion without any motive of gain, which does not even seek liberation.

equivalents.note: both name the highest, desireless devotion beyond the guṇa-graded forms; the Kapila Gītā's devotee refuses oneness, whereas the Devī Gītā's supreme devotion ends in non-dual knowledge

definitions.definition: The supreme 'I', spanning the letters from A (Śiva) to HA (Śakti) joined by the bindu (PTV).
The self as what the word and awareness 'I' refer to; not the ego-evolute of prakṛti but the soul itself, which persists as 'I' in deep sleep and liberation.
'I am Brahman' (BĀU 1.4.10): the realization sentence (anubhava-vākya), mahāvākya of the Yajurveda and of Śṛṅgeri.

The evolute of mahat whose nature is self-assertion (abhimāna); from it proceed the eleven organs (from its vaikṛta, sāttvika form) and the five subtle elements (from its bhūtādi, tāmasa form), both with its taijasa form (SK 24–25). It, not puruṣa, is the agent (SS 6.54).

Ego, one of the eight constituents of the lower nature (BhG 7.4); the deluded by ego think 'I am the doer' (3.27); free of 'mine' and ego one attains peace (2.71); in the Nārāyaṇīya, Aniruddha is called ahaṃkāra (12.327.26).

The I-maker: the 'teaching of I' (ahaṃkārādeśa) precedes the teaching of the self (ChU 7.25.1); listed among the faculties resting in the self (PrU 4.8); the jīva is endowed with intention and ahaṃkāra (ŚU 5.8).
The notion 'I' and 'mine', at whose arising the mind is to go to the supportless (VBT 131); in the Krama it is dissolved in the phases of Kālāgnirudra and Mahākāla (TĀ 4.161-168).

cross_language.note: also renders asmimāna; as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify

definitions.definition: Meditation on the object as oneself ('I am Brahman'), as opposed to symbol-meditation (BS 4.1.3).
The ego, the I-maker: the inner organ as appropriating ('I', 'mine'), the knot of superimposition of consciousness and the insentient.
The false notion of 'I' regarding body and the like, which ceases through knowledge of the truth about the causes of the faults (NS 4.2.1) and through contemplation of the body within (NBh 4.2.2).
An evolute of prakṛti; distinct from the true 'I' (aham-artha), which is the self; the false identification of body as self is the obstacle.

notes: Not the Sāṃkhya evolute; here a mistaken cognition.

definitions.definition: Food, which is threefold by the guṇas: life-giving, savoury and wholesome for the sāttvic; bitter, sour and burning for the rājasic; stale and impure for the tāmasic (BhG 17.7–10).
Purity of food (or of what is taken in): from it purity of mind, firm memory and the loosening of all knots (ChU 7.26.2).
The eastern fire into which oblations are offered.
Not injuring any being in any way at any time; the root of the other restraints and observances (YBh 2.30); when established, hostility is abandoned in one's presence (2.35).

Non-violence, 'the highest dharma for all beings that breathe' (MBh 1.11.12; 13.116); a mark of knowledge (BhG 13.7) and of the divine endowment (16.2); the eternal dharma taught by Tulādhāra (12.253–256); yet the meat-seller teaches that no one lives without some harm (3.199).
The ekāntins are non-violent; worship without animal slaughter (MBh 12.336.58; 12.323–324).
Non-injury, first of the common duties of all classes (MDh 10.63; YS 1.122; Arthaśāstra 1.3.13); the Veda-prescribed injury is declared to be non-injury (MDh 5.44).
Violence is prohibited; hence the Śyena rite, whose aim is violence, is harmful (anartha) though the Veda states it as a means for one who wishes to harm (Śabara on MS 1.1.2).

cross_language.note: first Jain vow

definitions.definition: The two qualities seen means lack (SK 1) and final isolation has (SK 68): certain (invariable) and final (without recurrence).
The doctrine that the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā (on ritual) and the Uttara Mīmāṃsā (on Brahman), with the Saṅkarṣa-kāṇḍa, form one continuous science.
The sixth sthala: free of longing for the droplets of sense-pleasure, pure of intent, immersed in the ocean of Śiva's bliss (SSM 14.2; 14.4); in common usage also the devotee's death (liṅgaikya).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) giving non-obstruction (SK 45); the commentaries list eight powers — becoming minute (aṇimā), great, light, reaching, irresistible will, lordship, control and going wherever one wishes. In Sāṃkhya these powers are aiśvarya, not 'siddhi'; attachment to them is the error called moha.

The eight lordly powers — minuteness, lightness, greatness, reach, irresistible will, control, lordship, and settling things at will (YBh 3.45); Īśvara's lordship, which has no equal or superior (YBh 1.24).
Proposed as a means of knowledge; not different from verbal testimony (NS 2.2.2).
The unborn (she-goat): one unborn female, red, white and black, producing many like herself, and two unborn males who enjoy and leave her (ŚU 4.5; cf. 1.9).

literal: the unborn part (or: the goat as portion)

definitions.definition: What Agni is asked to heat and carry to the world of the well-doers at cremation (RV 10.16.4); read either as the dead man's unborn part or as the goat offered as Agni's portion.
The python's way of living: accepting whatever food comes unsought, lying still if none comes.
Living like a python on whatever comes unsought, without striving (MBh 12.172).
Non-exclusive implication, which retains the direct meaning and adds to it ('the red runs' = the red horse); rejected for 'tat tvam asi'.
The mantra 'recited' by the breath without effort (ajapā-gāyatrī).
The spontaneous japa of the breath, 21,600 per day and night, the Goddess's japa (VBT 156).
The doctrine of non-origination: nothing whatever is ever born; creation-teachings are only means; the highest truth of Gauḍapāda.
The centre in the head, between the brows.
The tāmasa opposite of knowledge (SK 23); from it (viparyaya) comes bondage (SK 44).
Ignorance, synonym of avidyā: 'something positive, indescribable as being or non-being, made of the three guṇas, opposed to knowledge' (Vedāntasāra).
Not the absence of knowledge but incomplete manifestation of the knowable (TĀ 1.25-26); twofold, in the intellect and in the person, the latter the root of saṃsāra (Tantrasāra 1).
A stage of ignorance; seven are taught: seed-waking, waking, great waking, waking-dream, dream, dream-waking and deep sleep, each branching a hundredfold.
The mutual need of the parts of a sentence, which makes them one sentence (MS 2.1.46).
A word's inability to produce a connected cognition without another word (Tarkasaṅgraha).
Inaction, which the wise see in action and whose presence in inaction they also see (BhG 4.18); attachment to inaction is forbidden (2.47).
Puruṣa is non-agent (SK 19); agency belongs to the guṇas and puruṣa only appears as agent (SK 20); ahaṃkāra is the agent (SS 6.54).
One, all-pervading, eternal substance whose quality is sound.

Space: the final support from which all beings arise and into which they return (ChU 1.9.1); the accomplisher of name and form (ChU 8.14.1); the first element to arise from the self (TU 2.1); the space within the heart (ChU 8.1.3); 'kha' is brahman (ChU 4.10.4; BAU 5.1.1).

literal: mode in the form of the undivided

definitions.definition: The mental mode in the form of the partless Brahman arising from the mahāvākya; it destroys ignorance and then subsides, like a clearing-nut in water.
Partless meaning: a sentence that conveys a single non-relational entity, as the mahāvākya conveys the one self.
The verb, whose chief meaning is becoming (bhāva) as a sequence (Nirukta 1.1).
Error is not the appearance of an unreal object but the non-apprehension of the difference between a perception ('this') and a memory ('silver'); ignorance itself is non-apprehension.
Destitution of any means of one's own — no ritual merit, self-knowledge or devotion — the qualification for surrender.
Said of activities that have discernment as their object and oppose the operation of the guṇas (YBh 1.5).

literal: receiving (the fruit of) what was not done

definitions.definition: The absurdity of reaping results of acts one did not do — used to refute rival accounts of embodiment and of the agent (NS 3.2.38, 3.2.72 DCS).
The universal, which is what a word means, because Vedic action is directed to it (MS 1.3.33).
What is called the mark of the universal (NS 2.2.70 DCS).
Rosary into whose beads the fifty letters a–kṣa are invoked.
Lakṣmī, whose body is imperishable; beyond her is Hari (Puruṣottama).

The imperishable: that on which space is woven, described by negations (BAU 3.8.8), by whose command sun and moon stand apart (3.8.9); the object of the higher knowledge (MuU 1.1.5); also 'syllable', especially Om (ChU 1.1.1; KU 1.2.16; MāU 1).
The syllable in the highest heaven on which the verses rest and the gods sit (RV 1.164.39); the thousand-syllabled cow of speech (1.164.41).

The imperishable supreme Brahman (BhG 8.3), the goal entered by ascetics (8.11); the unchanging (kūṭastha) imperishable puruṣa (15.16), surpassed by the highest person (15.18); also the syllable (Oṃ, 'the one syllable', 8.13, 10.25).
A syllable or phoneme (akṣarasamāmnāya, the list of phonemes, PŚ 57).
The imperishable syllable Oṃ, which is Brahman and Prajāpati, while all rites pass away (MDh 2.84).
The imperishable Brahman, Puruṣottama's abode and 'feet', the goal of knowers; lower than Puruṣottama.
Śiva as beyond the kula; the Akula abode into which full consciousness finally dissolves (TĀ 4.170).
Taking no interest (seeking no gain) even in the highest reflection (4.29, YBh 4.29).
Failure to attain a stage of samādhi (YBh 1.30).
The support or object on which the mind rests (1.10, 1.38); samādhis with a support are samprajñāta (YBh 1.17).
Laziness: inactivity from heaviness of body and mind (YBh 1.30).

Perception through an extraordinary contact: through the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇā — grasping all smoke via smoke-hood, which grounds pervasion), through a prior cognition (jñānalakṣaṇā — e.g. 'fragrant sandal' seen), and yogic (yogaja).
Supernatural capacity to relish the Lord's bliss, the highest fruit of service.
The fourth level: the unmanifest pradhāna, subtlest of objects, beyond which nothing is subtler (1.45, 2.19).
The function of the sense capacities: mere awareness of sound and the rest (SK 28).
The initial non-conceptual awareness (ŚV pratyakṣa 112).
The later (uttara) tāraka, in which the mind is like an udder after milking.
The superhuman being who, at the lightning, leads the soul to Brahman.
The state of no-mind: when, through knowing the truth of the self, the mind ceases to imagine, grasping nothing (GK 3.32).
Distress or anxiety, from which Rudra and the gods are asked to set one free (RV 2.33.2).
Its authority follows from its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3).
One of the four cardinal monasteries founded, in the tradition's account, by Śaṅkara, each tied to a Veda, a mahāvākya and a group of Daśanāmī names.
Immortality and the immortal: of the gods, of the fathers' world, of soma; 'may I be freed from death, not from immortality' (RV 7.59.12).

equivalents.note: The Saṃhitās' immortality is chiefly full life and the immortal world of light; the Upaniṣads and Vedānta distinguish mokṣa from heavenly immortality. Recorded as contested.

definitions.definition: Immortality: the goal named by the early Upaniṣads — 'there is no hope of immortality through wealth' (BAU 2.4.2); 'so much is immortality' (4.5.15); 'the mortal becomes immortal' (4.4.7; KU 2.3.14); 'lead me from death to immortality' (BAU 1.3.28).

cross_language.note: Buddhist epithet of nibbāna

equivalents.note: the early texts' 'immortality' is what the later texts (ŚU 6.16, MaiU 6.20) call mokṣa; the early texts do not themselves equate the two words

definitions.definition: The eternal portion of the Lord that becomes the living being (BhG 15.7); the fragment of his splendour from which every glory springs (10.41–42).
The soul as a part of Brahman made distinct by adjuncts.
The soul as a naturally distinct part (power) of the Lord.
The soul as a spark-like part of Brahman in which bliss is concealed.
The soul as a separated part (vibhinnāṃśa), distinct from the Lord's own expansions (svāṃśa).

notes: Read as a real part or as an apparent part according to school (see dsp:souls-one-or-distinct).

definitions.definition: Worship of Viṣṇu through fire offerings, without an image.
The vowelless (and consonantless, ahala) sound meditated while closing ears and lower door (VBT 114); used in cutting the flows of breath (Kṣemarāja on PH 18).
The novelty required of a means of knowledge: it apprehends what was not apprehended before (Śāstradīpikā).
A form of non-knowledge — cognition that fails to determine its object ('what is this?') (Praśastapāda).
Days and circumstances (storms, deaths, festivals, the moon's days) on which Vedic recitation is suspended (MDh 4.101–127).
'Free from beginningless time': Śiva, never bound, distinguished from liberated souls who were once bound.
Freed from offence 'before Aditi', the state asked of Varuṇa when his fetters are loosened (RV 1.24.15).
The unstruck sound heard within; also the heart centre.
The unstruck, unbroken inner sound, the Sound-Brahman (VBT 38).

notes: In haṭha sources anāhata is also the heart-cakra; here the unstruck sound.

definitions.definition: The tāmasa opposite of power (SK 23), bringing obstruction (SK 45).
The essence of bondage for Kauṇḍinya: the soul's lack of lordship, the obstruction of its powers; also listed by him as the fifth impurity.
The nameless phase beyond emission, persistence and withdrawal in the Krama sequence.
Joy (hlāda), the third level of samprajñāta samādhi (1.17, YBh 1.17); Vijñānabhikṣu: a joy arising from preponderant sattva; Bhoja: bliss when the inner organ's sattva is cultivated.
Bliss produced by soma (RV 9.113.6) and dwelling in the immortal world (9.113.11).
Bliss: the nature of Brahman, not a quality it has; worldly joys are fragments of it, manifest in deep sleep as unobstructed bliss.

Bliss: brahman is bliss (TU 3.6); the self made of bliss (TU 2.5); brahman is understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28); the highest bliss of the brahma-world on a fraction of which others live (BAU 4.3.32); measured in the calculus of bliss (TU 2.8; BAU 4.3.33).
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the śaraṇa stage. In the SSM the śaraṇa is one possessed of the bliss of union with Śiva (13.2).
Bliss as the power of the Lord and as the relish of consciousness in pleasure, reunion, taste and song (VBT 65-74); seven grades in the contemplation of the breath (TĀ 5.43-52).
The dance of bliss of Naṭarāja at Chidambaram, enacting the five acts.
The gradation of the bliss enjoyed by the liberated, each class a hundredfold above the one below.
Made of bliss: the innermost of the five selves, whose tail and foundation is brahman (TU 2.5).
The sheath of bliss: ignorance (the causal body) with its joys experienced in deep sleep and in pleasure; for Śaṅkara a sheath, not Brahman (BSBh 1.1.19).
Devotion directed to nothing else, by which the supreme person is won (BhG 8.22), the Lord seen in truth (11.54) and gain and security borne (9.22).
Seeking nothing from the Lord but the Lord himself and his service.
Having no other refuge or goal than the Lord; with ākiñcanya the qualification for surrender.
The soul's being fit to belong to the Lord alone, not to itself nor to any other being; taught in the praṇava of the tirumantra.
An unwanted thing obstructing devotion; of four kinds by origin (sin, pious acts, offences, devotion itself).
Cessation of unwanted things (anartha) — the fourth stage.
The mind born of meditation, which lays down no karmic residue (4.6, YBh 4.6).
The impurity of individuality: loss of freedom by awareness, or awareness without freedom (ĪPK 3.2.4); 'limited knowledge is bondage' (Śiva Sūtra 1.2).
The impurity by whose contact the self, resting in the inner organ, has become atomic (aṇu) (SSM 18.5–7).
The innate (sahaja) impurity of the soul, one in substance with countless powers, beginningless, covering its powers of knowing and acting; it ripens and is removed by Śiva's power in initiation.
Āṇavam, the 'dark mala' (iruḷ mala) which hides even itself; never destroyed, only rendered powerless by grace.

notes: Same name as in the Śaiva Siddhānta, where the impurity is held to be a real substance.

definitions.definition: The mind's not being established in a stage it has gained (YBh 1.30).
The individual means: breath, bodily seals, visualization, letters and places (MVT 2.21; TĀ 5).
The eternal state of sorrow without return reached by the souls fit for darkness, especially through hatred of Hari and his devotees.
The fifth error, eighteenfold: the despair of one who dies amid, or falls from, the powers and objects (SK 48; Gauḍapāda; Kramadīpikā).
The doctrine of many jīvas, each with its own ignorance or inner organ, so that one is liberated while others remain bound (Bhāmatī and most Advaitins).

The soul or devotee in relation to the liṅga: knowledge is the aṅga and the eternal knowable the liṅga, and the aṅgaliṅgī has the liṅga mounted on the aṅga and the aṅga present in the liṅga (SSM 12.42–44); the jīva is a part of Śiva through beginningless ignorance (5.34–36).
A subsidiary element of a principal rite (pradhāna), e.g. the prayājas of the new- and full-moon rites.
What shakes the limbs, an accompaniment of distraction (YBh 1.31); steady posture prevents it (YBh 2.47).
The Aṅgirases, ancient priestly clan; with the Atharvans the Atharvaveda is 'Atharvāṅgirasaḥ'.
The subtle being, the size of a thumb, drawn out of the body at death by Yama's messengers.
The person the size of a thumb, dwelling in the middle of the body or the heart, lord of past and future (KU 2.1.12-13, 2.3.17; ŚU 3.13, 5.8).
The fourth form, from whom Brahmā arises; called the great self and ahaṃkāra (MBh 12.326.69; 12.327.26).
The vyūha manifesting power and splendour; in Śaṅkara's report, identified with ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
The fifth of the five forms of Viṣṇu invoked in Vaikhānasa worship.

equivalents.note: the Nārāyaṇīya calls Aniruddha ahaṃkāra

definitions.definition: The Advaita category of what is neither real nor unreal; for Dvaita it is established by no means of knowledge and taught by no scripture.
Indescribable: not determinable as real (since sublated) nor as unreal (since it appears); the status of māyā, avidyā and their products.
The Advaita theory of error: the illusory object (shell-silver) is neither real nor unreal but indescribable, produced for the moment by ignorance.
The signature name for the Lord that closes a vacanakāra's vacanas — Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva (Basava), Guhēśvara (Allama), Cennamallikārjuna (Akka), Rāmanātha (Dāsimayya) — usually received from the guru.
Food: brahman is food (TU 3.2); the person is made of the essence of food (TU 2.1); vows about food (TU 3.7-10); mind is made of food (ChU 6.5.4, 6.7); 'I am food' sings the knower (TU 3.10.6).
Made of (the essence of) food: the outermost self, the person formed from food (TU 2.1).
The sheath made of food: the gross body.
Love for Śiva, which is itself Śiva (Tirumantiram 270).
In the Kuṟaḷ (ch. 8), love that makes one belong to others; without it the body is bone wrapped in skin.

equivalents.note: aṉpu is love in general as well as devotion

definitions.definition: Non-cruelty, named the highest dharma by Yudhiṣṭhira to the Yakṣa (MBh 3.297.55, 3.297.71) and by the meat-seller (3.203.41); the reason Yudhiṣṭhira will not abandon the dog (17.3.7).
Untruth and violation of ṛta; what Varuṇa's fetters punish (AVŚ 4.16.6); even sleep does not keep it away (RV 7.86.6).
Buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas, the threefold internal instrument operating in all three times; the door-keeper, of which the ten external instruments are the doors (SK 33, 35).

The inner organ, one in substance and fourfold in function — mind (manas, doubting), intellect (buddhi, deciding), memory-store (citta) and ego (ahaṅkāra); the adjunct through which consciousness becomes the knower.
Mind and the rest, which one contemplates as absent in oneself (VBT 94).

literal: the time of the end, the hour of death

definitions.definition: The hour of death, when the state remembered determines where one goes (BhG 8.5–6); being in the brāhmī state even then brings brahmanirvāṇa (2.72).
The inner fire-offering of Pratardana: offering breath into speech while speaking and speech into breath while breathing, continually, waking or asleep (KauU 2.5).
Concentration, meditation and samādhi, inner relative to the first five limbs (3.7).
The Lord's internal, essential power, of three aspects (sandhinī, saṃvit, hlādinī), which constitutes his form, abode and associates.
An obstacle on the path of yoga; the ten of LiP 1.9 and ŚiP 7.2.38; the powers themselves are antarāyas (BhP 11.15.33).
The nine obstacles, distractions of the mind (1.30), removed through devotion to Īśvara (1.29) and practice on a single principle (1.32).
The atmosphere between earth and heaven, the middle of the three worlds.
Mental worship of the deity in the heart and body before external worship.
Mental worship (mānasayāga) preceding external worship.

literal: the one who controls from within

definitions.definition: The inner controller: 'he who dwells in the earth yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who controls it from within' — the self, the immortal (BAU 3.7).
The Lord dwelling within every soul and thing as its self and controller, and, in a special form, in the heart of the meditator.
The Lord dwelling within beings, one of his five modes.
The inner controller: Īśvara as the consciousness governing each being from within (BĀU 3.7), the 'starched canvas' of the Citradīpa.
Remembering the Lord at the moment of death; required of the bhakti-yogin but not of the surrendered, whom the Lord remembers.
The funeral rite — cremation (or burial of infants), bone-collection, water-offerings and the rites of the first year.
Minute, 'smaller than the small': the self in the heart smaller than a grain yet greater than the worlds (ChU 3.14.3; KU 1.2.20; ŚU 3.20).
The soul is atomic in size, dwelling in the heart and pervading the body by its quality of knowledge.
The soul is atomic, a spark of Brahman.
The soul is an infinitesimal particle of consciousness (cit-kaṇa).
The four preliminaries of a teaching text: qualified student, subject, relation and purpose.
Cognition other than memory; valid or invalid (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The outward expressions of emotion: dancing, rolling, singing, crying out, and the like.

In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the prāṇaliṅgi stage. More widely, lived experience of Śiva — the authority the śaraṇas appeal to, which gave the Anubhava Maṇṭapa its name.
The assembly at Kalyāṇa where, in the tradition's account, the śaraṇas of every birth and both sexes discussed their experience of Śiva under Allama's presidency.
Cognition other than memory; every experience is a means of knowledge (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Experience/awareness itself, the self as pure self-established consciousness (Iṣṭasiddhi).
One learned in the Veda, who is 'great among us' regardless of age or wealth (MDh 2.154).
The low accent.
The Lord's fifth power/act — grace — called compassion (kṛpā) and śaktipāta; one of Lakṣmī's five acts.
The Lord's favouring of the effect; also the teacher's right favour to qualified disciples, which preserves the tradition and itself leads to the end of suffering.
The Lord's grace, identical with puṣṭi.
A topic of the Tattvasamāsa (17); in the Kramadīpikā, Brahmā's creation, from the subtle elements, of provision for the beings he had produced.
An index of seers, deities, metres and hymns of a Veda (e.g. the Sarvānukramaṇī).
Favourableness: devotion is cultivation of Kṛṣṇa in a way pleasing to him (not as enemies 'think' of him).
The resolve to do only what pleases the Lord; first limb of prapatti.
Faultless reasoning (upapatti) based on invariable concomitance; includes presumption and comparison.
Threefold inference preceded by knowledge of the mark and the marked (SK 5); by inference from general correlation supersensible things (prakṛti, puruṣa) are known (SK 6).
Inference: an activity that chiefly ascertains the general through a relation present in like and absent from unlike cases (YBh 1.7); it reaches only the general (1.49, YBh 1.25).
Knowledge preceded by perception, of three kinds (NS 1.1.5); resting on perception and scripture it is anvīkṣā (NBh 1.1.1).
Knowledge from a mark (laiṅgika): effect, cause, connected, co-inherent, opposed (VS 9.18); includes verbal knowledge.
The instrument of inferential cognition, i.e. consideration (parāmarśa); for oneself or for others.
Cognition of an unperceived part from seeing another part whose relation is known; of two kinds, by a relation seen directly or by one seen in general (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
The cognition produced by consideration (parāmarśa).
Another name for the sixth means of knowledge, by which absence is known.
Proposed (as 'abhāva') as a separate means of knowledge; not different from inference (NS 2.2.2); later, absence is perceived through the qualifier-relation contact.
Non-cognition: the means by which absence is known (a jar's absence on the ground), accepted as a separate means following Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā.
The 'means-less': realization by the teacher's word alone for the most intensely graced (TĀ 2).
The means that produce valid knowledge: perception, inference and authoritative word (presumption and comparison fall under inference).
Ever-new passion in which the beloved is experienced as ever fresh.
A further ash-bath after impurities such as eating, sneezing, spitting or evacuation, for purity and to show the sign; a secondary rule.

literal: known from what is heard (the Veda)

definitions.definition: The Vedic ritual means, which are like the seen means because impure, perishable and graded (SK 2).
The metre of four eight-syllable lines (the Puruṣa Sūkta's metre), later the śloka.
A Vedic metre of 32 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
The Unsurpassed: the supreme reality of the Trika, identified with the letter A and with the Heart; Parātrīśikā's question concerns how the anuttara grants immediate Kaula perfection.

literal: unsurpassed; that beyond which there is nothing

definitions.definition: The soul's atomic size: it dwells in the heart and pervades the body by its attributive consciousness.
An arthavāda stating what is already known by another means of knowledge (e.g. that fire is a remedy for cold).
Repetition of what has been enjoined, distinct from mere repetition (NS 2.1.66–68 DCS).
A lesson or section, the recitation unit of the Ṛgveda (within maṇḍalas) and of the Taittirīya texts.
A mental perception, following a cognition, of the form 'I know this'; the means by which a cognition is known, since a cognition does not reveal itself.
The reflective cognition 'I know this' that follows a cognition; for Murāri Miśra it grasps the first cognition's validity (as reported by Gaṅgeśa).
The locus in which a relation or absence is (the ground, for 'absence of pot on the ground').
A probans with both positive and negative concomitance, e.g. smoke for fire.
The science of reasoning, the fourth of the four sciences, 'the lamp of all sciences' (NBh 1.1.1).
Words express their meanings only as already connected with other meanings, ultimately with what is to be done (kārya), as learned from elders' usage.
Free from desires other than for Kṛṣṇa's service — the first mark of pure devotion.
Wrong knowledge — for Madhva the real sense of 'dvaita' in the Māṇḍūkya: the soul's misapprehension (of its relation to the body and to God), which ceases by God's will when he is known.
The Nyāya theory of error: a thing is cognized as qualified by a property it lacks — the silver seen elsewhere is presented in the mother-of-pearl.
An invariable antecedent that is nevertheless not a cause (e.g. the colour of the potter's staff).
Absence whose counterpositive is delimited by identity ('a pot is not cloth').
Substance with cold touch, fluid and viscid; bodies of water in Varuṇa's world.
Conduct permitted when normal dharma cannot be kept, illustrated by Viśvāmitra in famine (MBh 12.139).
The relaxed rules of livelihood and conduct permitted in emergencies (MDh 10.81ff.).
One of the five vital winds that are the shared function of the three internal instruments (SK 29); the Kramadīpikā places it at the navel.
The complementary breath to prāṇa in the Gītā's breath-sacrifice (BhG 4.29) and equalization (5.27).
The downward (or out-) breath; in PrU 3.5 it is in the organs of excretion and generation; the navel's function whose deity is death (AU 1.1.4).
Out-breath, named with prāṇa in the Saṃhitā lists of breaths (TS 4.7; AVŚ 8.1, 15.16).
The downward breath, seated at the anus.
The Lord's eightfold divided nature: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego (BhG 7.4).
The lower knowledge: the four Vedas and the six ancillary sciences (MuU 1.1.5).
Not appropriating objects, seeing the faults of acquiring, keeping, losing, attachment and harm (YBh 2.30); when steady, knowledge of the how of births (2.39).

cross_language.note: fifth Jain vow

definitions.definition: Direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of God — in the form of one's own original (bimba), to the extent one's fitness allows — produced by meditation built on hearing and reflection.
Immediate knowledge: knowledge of the self as oneself ('you are the tenth'); for the Vivaraṇa produced by the mahāvākya directly.

equivalents.note: Dvaita uses aparokṣa-jñāna and sākṣātkāra (direct realization) of God interchangeably.

definitions.definition: The Veda's character of having no author, not even God; its words and order are eternal.
The Veda as not composed by any person; the named seers saw or first transmitted it.
Mīmāṃsā's claim that the Veda has no author, rejected by Nyāya: the Veda is composed with understanding and its validity comes from its reliable author.

notes: The term is Mīmāṃsā's (U12); the Saṃhitā lineage's self-understanding is recorded here with the counter-evidence of 'fashioned' hymns (dsp:seen-or-made-hymns).

definitions.definition: The Veda's having no author, human or divine; names like Kāṭhaka come from expounding, not authorship (MS 1.1.30); the unbroken chain of teachers' study has no first term (ŚV vākya 366); since defects of testimony depend on speakers, an authorless Veda is free of them (ŚV codanā 62).
Retraction: showing that what was superimposed is nothing but its substratum, as the snake is only the rope.
Absolute release from pain (NS 1.1.22), reached when false knowledge and the rest are removed (NS 1.1.2); on the mainstream view without pleasure or cognition (NBh 1.1.22).
Liberation, which comes through knowledge (SK 44); defined in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra as the indifference of one of the two (SS 3.66).
Liberation as the second purpose of the seen: determining the enjoyer's own nature (2.18, YBh 2.18).

equivalents.note: Within Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, apavarga, mokṣa, mukti and niḥśreyasa (in its final sense) name the same state.
Sāṃkhya-Yoga's isolation of puruṣa is also a state without pain and without objects; but Nyāya's self is a substance whose consciousness is adventitious, while puruṣa is consciousness itself.

definitions.definition: The cognition 'this is one, this is one' that produces duality and higher numbers in things; its role at creation (for the magnitude of dyads) is one of Udayana's proofs of the Lord.
One of the Lord's three powers with cognition and memory (ĪPK 1.3.7); every determinate awareness arises by exclusion of an opposite (1.6.5) - a reworking of the Buddhist apoha.
Non-material 'matter': the substance of the Lord's form and abode, beyond prakṛti.
Transcendental, not of māyā: the Lord's body, name and abode and the devotee's perfected body.
Heedfulness, declared by Sanatsujāta to be immortality (MBh 5.42.4); one of the three 'horses of Brahman' with self-restraint and renunciation (11.7.19; 5.43.14).
Attentiveness to what is to come, like guarding a sprout; a niyama, the fifth strength, and the state in which the end of suffering is reached.

cross_language.note: cognate; the Dhammapada's 'appamādo amatapadaṃ' is recorded by the Buddhist units

definitions.definition: The unmanifest (prakṛti), which does not awaken, and the self while it has not awakened (MBh 12.292–296).

The relation of inseparable existence between a substance and its mode (as between Brahman and souls/matter, or a substance and its attribute): the mode can neither exist nor be known apart from the substrate, yet is distinct from it.

One who has directly experienced the thing and speaks from the wish to communicate it as seen — the same definition for seers, āryas and mlecchas (NBh 1.1.7); the Veda is valid because its seers and teachers are reliable (NS 2.1.69).
One who speaks of things as they are (yathārthavaktā) (Tarkasaṅgraha).

Reliable testimony (reliable revelation, SK 5), establishing what neither perception nor inference establishes (SK 6); the reliable person is devoted to his work, free of passion and aversion, knowing and virtuous (Kramadīpikā).
Non-return to rebirth, reached by those who come to the Lord (BhG 8.15–16), by knowers who depart on the bright path (8.24), and by the knowers of the self (5.17).
The unseen potency brought about by a perishable ritual act, postulated because the fruit (e.g. heaven) comes later: 'there is an apūrva, since the undertaking is enjoined' (Śabara on MS 2.1.5).
A capacity produced in the self (or the act) by the rite; later Bhāṭṭas distinguish the final apūrva of the fruit from those of the parts and subsidiaries.
The apūrva is the 'what is to be done' (kārya/niyoga) made known by the injunction itself, knowable only from the Veda.

equivalents.note: Both name the unseen result of acts that ripens later; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika places adṛṣṭa in the self and makes Īśvara its overseer, which Mīmāṃsā rejects

notes: The Bhāṭṭa subdivision of apūrvas (e.g. phala-, samudāya-, utpatti-, aṅga-apūrva) is from memory (low); not attached to a teaching.

definitions.definition: An injunction of what is not obtained by any other means at all (e.g. sprinkling the rice).
A subsidiary enjoined by itself, not with reference to a material (e.g. the prayājas), helping only toward the final apūrva.
The hereditary temple performance of the Prabandham in song, gesture and dance by the araiyars, traced to Nāthamuni.
Virtue, righteousness; first of the Kuṟaḷ's three books; 'being spotless in mind is the whole of aṟam' (Kuṟaḷ 34).

equivalents.note: aṟam centres on inner purity and non-harm; dharma includes ritual duty

definitions.definition: First of the four stages of yoga.
The effect is a new beginning, not pre-existing in its material cause (the whole produced by the parts is a new substance).

literal: to be sung in the forest

definitions.definition: The melodies sung in the forest, regarded as more potent and secret.
A 'forest book' of a Vedic school, containing the dangerous or secret rites and meditations (Mahāvrata, Pravargya, saṃhitā-upaniṣads) studied away from the village, and often an Upaniṣad.
The Lord's descent into consecrated images in temples and homes, the most accessible of his forms, where he depends even on his worshippers.
The Lord present in a consecrated image, the most accessible of his five modes.
The image of Viṣṇu in which he is worshipped; image worship is the best means.
Hereditary Vaikhānasa priest serving a Viṣṇu temple.
Temple priest (in Tamil Śaiva usage the Ādiśaiva/Śivācārya).
Ritual worship of the Lord, the fifth form of devotion; the chief means in the Dvāpara age.
A verse-book of the Sāmaveda (Pūrvārcika, Uttarārcika), the texts on which the melodies are sung.
The path of the gods by which the freed soul travels from the body to Vaikuṇṭha, escorted by the deities of light, day, the bright fortnight, the northern course, the year and the rest.
The path 'beginning with light': the stations of the path of the gods (BS 4.3.1–6).
The path by which the knowers go to Brahmā's world, from which they reach the Supreme with Brahmā at the great dissolution.
The fourth, half measure of Oṃ, beyond the guṇas and beyond speech, touched at the crown (MkP 42.5-6, 42.14).
The subtle fourth element of Oṃ beyond a, u and m; the 'head' of the Oṃ-bird.
Signs of approaching death, personal, from other beings, or from the gods (YBh 3.22).
A sign foretelling death, by which yogins know their time (e.g. no longer seeing Arundhatī or the pole-star).
Omen foretelling death.
Offering to the liṅga everything meant for one's own enjoyment before enjoying it, so that all is received as prasāda (SSM 11.6–11).
Knowledge of seers arising from particular merits (VS 9.28 C); intuitive knowledge of past, future and supersensible things in the seers (Praśastapāda).
One who, unable to bear saṃsāra, asks for release at once, at the end of this body.
Wealth and power, the livelihood of the world, the aim served by the Arthaśāstra.

notes: Its sense 'meaning' (of a word) is used in the Vedāṅgas (Nirukta 2.1: 'attend always to the meaning').

definitions.definition: Knowledge of the self, the Lord, the means, the goal and the obstacle — the content a seeker must learn from the teacher.

literal: the five things to be known

definitions.definition: The five things to be known: the worshipped (upāsya), the worshipper (upāsaka), the fruit of grace, the rasa of devotion, and the obstacles.

notes: The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition has its own arthapañcaka (Piḷḷai Lokācārya); definitions differ.

definitions.definition: Supposing an unseen fact without which a seen or heard fact would not be possible (Devadatta, alive and not at home, is outside) — the Vṛttikāra in Śabara; accepted by both Bhāṭṭas and Prābhākaras.
Proposed as a means of knowledge; included in inference (NS 2.2.2).
Included in inference (Praśastapāda).
Presumption: knowing what must be so to account for something otherwise inexplicable (fat Devadatta who does not eat by day eats at night).

Vedic passages that do not themselves enjoin; they are meaningful as praise of what is enjoined, forming one sentence with the injunctions (MS 1.2.7). A fruit stated for a subsidiary is arthavāda (MS 4.3.1).

A sentence whose purport is praise or blame; supplementing an injunction or a prohibition; classified as praise, blame, another's deed and ancient narrative, or as figurative (guṇavāda), restating (anuvāda) and fact-stating (bhūtārthavāda).
The explanatory portion of a Brāhmaṇa (blame, praise, the deeds of others, ancient precedent) as distinct from injunction (ĀpŚS 24.1.33).
Vedic statements of praise, blame, another's practice and ancient precedent (NS 2.1.65 DCS).
The activity toward an act produced by the desire for a purpose, expressed by the verbal ending as such: 'one should bring about heaven by the sacrifice in this way'.
One who has taken the higher way of Śiva-worship and resorts again to lower practice (SSM 9.39–40).
Grace: Śiva's own power (aruḷ-catti) acting toward the soul; ever present, it removes the power of mala and comes as the guru.
The Lord's grace that saves the devotee from every danger and cuts births.
In the Kuṟaḷ, aruḷ is compassion for all living beings (chapter 25, Aruḷuṭaimai).

equivalents.note: aruḷ is also Śiva's power itself

definitions.definition: The Āḻvārs' hymns (Divya Prabandham) as graciously given; the Tamil Veda.
The sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, for whom action is the means (BhG 6.3).

The twenty-eight incapacities: injuries of the eleven organs (deafness, blindness, numbness, etc.) and seventeen injuries of buddhi, the reversals of the nine contentments and eight accomplishments (SK 49).
Attachment to the Lord that makes household life distasteful (Bhaktivardhinī).
The seventh stage: attachment to the Lord's name, qualities and abode.
A cause inhering in the same thing as the effect or its cause (conjunction of threads for cloth; colour of threads for cloth's colour).
The 'other' samādhi, preceded by practice of the cognition of cessation, with only impressions remaining (1.18); nothing is cognized in it (YBh 1.2); means: higher dispassion (YBh 1.18).
Fifth stage: from practice of the four, non-association with objects becomes firm and the wonder of sattva is established.
Fifth stage: non-attachment; the excellent knower.
Abstaining from worldly transactions; the fourth Pāśupata yama.
Posture; the Vāyavīya names eight (svastika, padma, ardhendu, vīra, yoga, prasādhita, paryaṅka, as one likes); the MkP names padma, half and svastika.
Posture is what is steady and pleasant (SS 3.34); there is no fixed rule (SS 6.24).
Posture, steady and comfortable (2.46), achieved by relaxing effort and coalescence with the endless (2.47); Vyāsa lists seated postures such as padmāsana, bhadrāsana and svastika (YBh 2.46).
Posture — four, eight, nine, eleven or seventeen named; inwardly, indifference or the seat where Brahman-thought flows.
Dishonour, declared the highest of all restraints; Kauṇḍinya: it removes pride of birth and of householder status.
Non-being or the non-existent, in which the seers found the bond of being (RV 10.129.4); from it being was born (10.72.2–3).
Non-being: some said this was non-being in the beginning (rejected in ChU 6.2.1-2); TU 2.7 and ChU 3.19.1 say non-being was first and being came from it.

equivalents.note: Śaṅkara reads the asat of creation texts as the unmanifest (unmanifested name and form), not absolute nothing; the Saṃhitā does not say so.

literal: doctrine that the effect is non-existent (before production)

definitions.definition: The rival (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika) view that the effect is new, rejected by Sāṃkhya: the non-existent cannot be produced, like a man's horn (SK 9; SS 1.114).
Before production the effect is non-existent (a prior absence of it is real) (NS 4.1.48–50; effect as counterpositive of prior absence, Tarkasaṅgraha).

equivalents.note: Opposed doctrines: Sāṃkhya's pre-existent effect.

definitions.definition: Uttering the words without delay.
The ritual impurity of relatives after a birth or death, lasting ten days for sapiṇḍas (MDh 5.59) or by class (5.83).
Three kinds: as to the locus (the sky-lotus), as to itself, as to pervasion (with an adjunct).
The self-wish 'may I not cease, may I be', eternal, which makes the latent tendencies beginningless (4.10, YBh 2.9, 4.10).

(1) The affliction: the seeming identity of the power of the seer and the power of seeing (2.6). (2) The fourth level of samprajñāta samādhi, awareness of a single self (YBh 1.17). (3) 'Asmitā-mātra', the sixth unparticularized principle (YBh 2.19) and the source of created minds (4.4).

equivalents.note: YBh 2.19 names the sixth unparticularized principle asmitā-mātra where Sāṃkhya names ahaṃkāra; Bhoja (RM 1.17) insists asmitā and ahaṃkāra are not the same.

definitions.definition: 'Contactless yoga': Gauḍapāda's discipline of the mind that realizes the unborn, free from contact with objects, feared by yogins who see fear where there is none.

One of the four orders: student, householder, forest-hermit, renouncer (MDh 6.87); whether they are chosen freely, followed in sequence, or whether only the householder's is Vedic is disputed (GDh 3.1–3.36; BDh 2.6.11.27; VDh 7.3; ĀpDh 2.9.21.1).

Stage of life: 'proceeding through one's own āśramas' is part of the remedy (MaiU 4.3); ŚU 6.21 names those beyond the āśramas (atyāśramin); ChU 2.23.1 has three 'branches of dharma' without the word.

literal: stage of exertion; order of life

definitions.definition: The eightfold daily play of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa from the end of night to night, the object of meditative remembrance (Govindalīlāmṛta, Kṛṣṇabhāvanāmṛta).
Viṣṇu's agency in the creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release of the world (Tattvasaṅkhyāna adds happiness, sorrow, covering and light).
The eight maṭhas of Uḍupi founded by Madhva's eight ascetic disciples.
The eight-ingredient binding compound that fixes the image to its pedestal, periodically renewed with rites.
Used likewise in Tamil temple practice (aṣṭabandhana).
The 'eight seals': the eight poet-singers of the Puṣṭimārga appointed by Viṭṭhalanātha — Sūrdās, Kumbhandās, Paramānanddās, Kṛṣṇadās, Nanddās, Caturbhujdās, Govindsvāmī, Chītsvāmī.
Earth and the other elements, sun, moon and the self as Śiva's eight forms — in the SSM his body and effect, over which he presides, neither non-different from him nor separate (10.48–52).
The eight limbs: restraints, observances, posture, breath-regulation, sense-withdrawal, concentration, meditation, samādhi (2.29), whose practice destroys impurity (2.28).
The eight protections of the Liṅgāyata: guru, liṅga, jaṅgama, pādōdaka, prasāda, vibhūti, rudrākṣa and mantra; several appear as sub-sthalas of the bhakta-sthala in the SSM (5.27–30).
Freedom from desire for what is not one's own (YBh 2.30); when established, all jewels present themselves (2.37).
One of the common duties of all (MDh 10.63).
The life-breath that leaves at death (the fathers 'have gone to asu', RV 10.15.1); the one life of the gods arose from the waters (10.121.7).
Viewing the body as hair, flesh, blood, bone, bile, excrement and so on, cultivated to abandon lustful passion (NBh 4.2.3).

cross_language.note: same term; the Buddhist practice has its own contexts and lists

definitions.definition: The karma of the yogin (4.7): not white, since he renounces the fruit; not black, since he does not take it up (YBh 4.7); others' karma is black, white-and-black, or white.
In the Ṛgveda a lord of mysterious power, applied to Varuṇa and other gods ('great is the one asura-ship of the gods', RV 3.55); later the gods' opponents.

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan ahura.

definitions.definition: Hypocrisy, arrogance, pride, anger, harshness and ignorance, leading to bondage (BhG 16.4–5); its bearers deny truth, foundation and a Lord (16.8).
The imperishable tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns, to be cut with the axe of non-attachment (BhG 15.1–4); 'among trees I am the aśvattha' (10.26).
The eternal fig tree with roots above and branches below, which is brahman, the immortal, in which all worlds rest (KU 2.3.1).
The twin horsemen, divine physicians and rescuers, praised by Ghoṣā (RV 10.39–40).
The primordial fire-priest who churned out Agni (RV 6.16.13); with the Aṅgirases, the seers of the Atharvaveda.

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan āθravan (priest).

definitions.definition: The old name of the Atharvaveda, pairing its auspicious (ātharvaṇa) and fierce (āṅgirasa) portions.
The gift of oneself to the Lord, whose fruit is final non-return, as against ordinary gifts of cows, land and gold.
The extension of the procedure of an archetype to an ectype ('the ectype is to be performed like the archetype'), in general (adhyāya 7) and in particular (adhyāya 8).

literal: one who has passed beyond what is to be cultivated

definitions.definition: One of Vyāsa's four kinds of yogin (YBh 3.51): One whose sole aim is the dissolution of the mind, with the sevenfold final insight.
Name given by the Śaiva scriptures to the Pāśupata and Lākula (and skull-observing) division of Śaivism: knowledge 'beyond the states of the intellect', 'beyond the world'.
In the Mantramārga's own scriptures, the ascetic Śaiva path (Pāśupata and Lākula) ranked above Vedic and 'spiritual' religion but below the Mantramārga.

notes: U17 owns lin:atimarga and its own account; this is the Mantramārga's classification.

definitions.definition: A Tamil Śaiva monastic house (maṭha) headed by a paṇṭāra-caṉṉiti, e.g. Tiruvāvaṭuturai and Dharmapuram, custodians of the Meykaṇṭa tradition and of temples.
Enduring the three sufferings without remedy while keeping one's rule; the supreme austerity.
The guest, whose honouring is the sacrifice to men (MDh 3.70).
The deities who conduct the departed soul along the path of light.
The airy (vāyavīya) body that the dead takes immediately upon leaving the gross body.
The knower beyond castes and stages of life.
Performing the prescribed acts as the Lord's command; the supreme worship.
'Those at the feet': Śiva's devotees, to be served and revered as Śiva himself.
The freed soul should join the true devotees (meyyaṭiyār) and revere their garb as Śiva.
The Śrīvaiṣṇava's customary way of saying 'I', expressing servitude.
Giving oneself over to the Lord's protection — the principal (aṅgin) of prapatti in Deśika's account, the sixth of the six in the Ahirbudhnya verse.
The renouncer's own funerary offering, among the eight śrāddhas.
Inquiry into the self: 'Who am I? How did this world arise? Who is its maker? What is its material?' (Aparokṣānubhūti 12); inquiry, not action, attains the Real (VC 11).
The highest dharma, attained by yoga (YS 1.8).
The eight virtues — compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, calm, auspiciousness, generosity, freedom from greed — without which the forty sacraments do not lead to Brahman (GDh 8.22–25).
The highest of the means to the supreme good, foremost of all sciences, by which immortality is gained (MDh 12.85).

The self: in the Upaniṣads the innermost reality of a person — the seer of seeing that cannot be seen (BAU 3.4.2), the inner controller (BAU 3.7), the light of a person (BAU 4.3.6) — which is declared to be brahman (BAU 1.4.10, 2.5.19; ChU 6.8.7; MāU 2). The word also means body or oneself in narrative passages (ChU 8.8.4).

Breath and self: Sūrya is the self of what moves and stands (RV 1.115.1); the dead man's breath (ātman) goes to the wind (10.16.3); Vāta is the self of the gods (10.168.4); knowing the wise, ageless, young self one does not fear death (AVŚ 10.8.44).

The embodied self, unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain (BhG 2.20); to be raised by the self, being its own friend or enemy (6.5–6); the Lord as the self in the heart of all beings (10.20).

An eternal substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition, known by the marks desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition (NS 1.1.10); the knower, the one who remembers (NS 3.2.40).
An all-pervading substance marked by breath, eye-movements, life, mind's movement, desire, effort etc. (VS 3.2.4 C); many (VS 3.2.16 C); perceived by yogins (VS 9.13).
The substrate of cognition; two kinds: the supreme self (the one omniscient Lord) and the individual self, distinct in each body, all-pervading and eternal (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The inner self (pratyag-ātman): pure, self-luminous consciousness, the witness of the three states, not the body, senses, mind or ego; identical with Brahman.

In ritual contexts the body or trunk (of the altar, of the sacrificer) that the rite constructs; in the teachings of Śāṇḍilya and Aśvapati the inner self 'made of mind, with breath for body' (ŚB 10.6.3).
The self to be seen by yoga (YS 1.8), its own witness (MDh 8.84), one in all beings though appearing many like space in pots (YS 3.144).
The one self of the deity of which the many gods are limbs (Nirukta 7.4).
The self, distinct from body and cognition, known to itself, shown by desire, memory and recognition; taught by negation ('not this, not this') (the Vṛttikāra in Śabara).
Distinct from cognition, senses and body; all-pervading, permanent, many; manifested as the subject in cognitions of objects (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Eternal, the agent and enjoyer who reaps the fruits of rites in another world; known through reasoning and made firm by the Upaniṣads (ŚV ātmavāda 148).

The eternal self, distinct from body, senses and intellect, known through the I-cognition and memory (SSM 5.55–60); dwelling in the heart like the hundredth part of a hair-tip, shining like a lamp (18.5–7).
The self is consciousness (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); the bound self is the mind (3.1); the self is a dancer (3.9).
U04 usage: the Self in the body-temple, identical with Brahman; threefold as outer, inner and supreme self in the Ātma Upaniṣad.

cross_language.note: the Buddhist texts deny a permanent attā; same word, opposed doctrine

definitions.definition: Complete self-surrender to the Lord, the ninth form of devotion.
Private worship by an initiate in the liṅga given by the guru or on a ground-altar, for one's own fruit.
Worship of Śiva for oneself, obligatory daily for the initiate.
The direct experience of one's own self as distinct from matter, the fruit of karma- and jñāna-yoga and prerequisite for bhakti-yoga.
One who sacrifices knowing that each rite builds a limb of his own (new) self, and who so sheds the mortal body like a snake its skin (ŚB 11.2.6.13).
One who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, and so attains self-rule (MDh 12.91).
Renunciation in mortal danger, by mind and speech.
Absence whose counterpositive is delimited by a relation for all three times ('no pot on the ground').
Final, without recurrence — of the cessation of suffering in kaivalya (SK 1, 68).
Liberation understood as a dissolution: knowledge cuts the ego-knot and the self abides in itself; dissolution into the eternal Brahman (VP 6.8.1).
Beyond the stages of life: the Pāśupata observance so described by revelation.
The Pāśupata state: the initiate leaves the rules of his former āśrama and follows the restraints and observances of the state beyond the āśramas.
Name used by Śaiva scripture for the Pāśupata branch of the Atimārga.
One beyond the stages of life, to whom Śvetāśvatara declared brahman (ŚU 6.21).
Bhāskara's form: difference of soul from Brahman is due to real limiting adjuncts (upādhi); non-difference is natural.
The relation of word and meaning, not created by any person (MS 1.1.5); known from the beginningless usage of elders (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Delimitation: consciousness delimited by the intellect, like the space enclosed by a pond; its identity with the whole is taught by the great sayings.
The Goddess appears divided by adjuncts like the space in pots.
Delimitation: the jīva as consciousness delimited by the inner organ, as space by a pot.
The property (or relation) by which a property or relation is specified — e.g. potness delimits the counterpositiveness of 'absence of pot'.
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the prasādi stage.
One who has 'shaken off' all worldly ties, a liberated wanderer who behaves like a child, madman or dullard; the teacher of King Yadu.

Defined syllable by syllable: a — free of the noose of hope, ever in bliss; va — free of vāsanās, living in the present; dhū — dust-grey limbs, cleansed mind, free of concentration and meditation; ta — held to truth, free of anxiety, darkness and ego.
The renouncer who has shaken off saṃsāra, beyond castes and stages, without marks or rules; etymologized syllable by syllable.
Inviting the deity into an image for worship; not done for the iṣṭaliṅga, in which Śiva already abides from initiation (SSM 10.44–47).
Being held in contempt by all beings, sought by the second-stage ascetic.
The veiling power of māyā that covers knowledge.
The veiling power of ignorance, which hides the self as a small cloud hides the sun from the viewer.
The practitioner's fixed stations until the gain: manifest, unmanifest, conquest, cutting, completion.
State of the soul: waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and beyond the fourth.
Avattai: the soul's states; also the three great conditions kēvalam (isolation with āṇava), cakalam (embodied) and cuttam (purified).
Change in the strength or condition of a present property (e.g. impressions of stilling growing strong; a pot's newness turning to age) (3.13, YBh 3.13, 3.15).
Viṣṇu's manifestation of his own eternal body of consciousness and bliss, not a birth of flesh; the avatāras are wholly identical with him and flawless.
The Lord's coming into being age after age by his own māyā to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (BhG 4.6–8); the noun itself is not used in the Gītā.
The Lord's successive manifestations (prādurbhāva), foretold by Nārāyaṇa to Nārada (MBh 12.326.72–94).

A descent of the Lord in a form for the protection of the world; innumerable, the principal ones listed as twenty-two (BhP 1.3), ten (Agni, Garuḍa) and in other lists; all are portions and parts, but Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself (BhP 1.3.28).
The Lord's real descent in a body of pure sattva by his own will, not from karma.
The uprooting of desire (Kuṟaḷ ch. 37), desire being the seed of all births.
(1) A member of the demonstrative statement — proposition, reason, example, application, conclusion (NS 1.1.32); (2) a part of a whole.
A part, in which the whole (avayavin) inheres.
A new substance over and above its parts, inhering in them and perceived (NS 2.1.31–37, 4.2.4–17).
The notion of the whole form (e.g. 'woman', 'man') with its embellishments that causes the faults (NS 4.2.3; NBh).
A rival account of liberation rejected by Rāmakaṇṭha: possession [of the soul by the Lord's qualities].
Among the siddha's powers: he 'enters all' and none can enter him (sarvāṃś cāviśati ... anāveśyaḥ).
Viṣṇu's special presence in a soul (as distinct from an avatāra); one must know which beings are his avatāras and which are only his āveśas.
Vijñānabhikṣu: non-separation — souls and prakṛti are not separate from Brahman, their substrate, though distinct; his preferred name for the relation.
The released soul's non-separation from Brahman (BS 4.4.4).

Taking the impermanent, impure, painful and non-self as permanent, pure, pleasant and self (2.5); the field of the other afflictions (2.4) and the cause of the conjunction (2.24); not the absence of knowledge but a contrary cognition (YBh 2.5).

Ignorance: in Śaṅkara, superimposition itself (the non-discrimination of self and not-self); in later Advaita, a beginningless, positive, indescribable power that veils Brahman and projects the world, removed by knowledge alone.
One positive ignorance having pure consciousness as its locus and object.
Ignorance residing in the individual selves (many, one per jīva), with Brahman as its object.

In the Tattvasamāsa, the five-jointed avidyā = the five errors (Tattvasamāsa 12; Kramadīpikā). The Sāṃkhya Sūtra denies that bondage is caused by an avidyā that is unreal (SS 1.20–26) or that avidyā is the world's material cause (SS 5.65).

Ignorance: those living in it think themselves wise and go round like the blind led by the blind (KU 1.2.5; MuU 1.2.8); Īśa 9-11 pairs it with vidyā (read by some as rites); the perishable is avidyā (ŚU 5.1); the teacher takes one across to the far shore of avidyā (PrU 6.8).
VP 6.7.11: taking non-self for self and what is not one's own as 'mine'; VP 1.5.5: fivefold avidyā arising first in creation; VP 6.7.61: the third, 'avidyā-karma' śakti.
A real, beginningless covering in each soul, twofold: one covering the soul's own nature and qualities, one covering (the soul's knowledge of) the Supreme; removed only by the Lord.
Defective cognition arising from defects of the senses and from impressions (VS 9.25–26 C); doubt, error, indefinite cognition and dream (Praśastapāda).

Not an indescribable cosmic ignorance but karma (the third power 'avidyā-karma' of Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.61) and the ignorance it causes in the soul — the contraction of its knowledge and the mistaking of body for self.

equivalents.note: Used interchangeably in Advaita texts (Vedāntasāra prefers ajñāna).

notes: Not the cosmic ignorance of Advaita.

definitions.definition: Unmodified transformation: Brahman becomes the world without any change in itself, as gold in ornaments.
Kāśī, where Rudra gives the tāraka to the dying; located in the body between brows and nose.
Non-abstention: the mind's greed for contact with objects (YBh 1.30).

Manifestation and concealment: Brahman's being, consciousness and bliss are manifest or concealed in its forms; creation and dissolution are manifestation and concealment, not origination and destruction.
The five subtle elements, which lack the calm, turbulent and dull differentiation (SK 38).
The second level: the five tanmātras and I-am-ness alone (2.19, YBh 2.19).
Inference proceeding by difference, negating (the alternatives) — the śeṣavat kind (Vācaspati on SK 5).
Uttering meaningless, repetitive or self-contradictory words.

notes: From the sūtra 'api tad bhāṣeta'.

definitions.definition: Acting as one who cannot tell pure from impure, fit from unfit (e.g. handling sticks and clods), without breaking the restraints.

notes: From the sūtra 'api tat kuryāt'; Ratnaṭīkā: apitatkaraṇa.

definitions.definition: The failure to discriminate puruṣa from prakṛti, the cause of their conjunction and so of bondage (SS 1.55); beginningless, removed by discrimination like darkness by light; bondage is non-discrimination alone (SS 6.12–16). The manifest and unmanifest are 'non-discriminating' (SK 11).

Prakṛti in its unmanifest state: uncaused, eternal, pervasive, inactive, one, unsupported, non-merging, partless and independent — the opposite of the manifest (SK 10) — and known through its effects (SK 8, 14–16).
The unmanifest: higher than the great self, below the person (KU 1.3.11, 2.3.8).

The unmanifest: from which beings emerge at Brahmā's day (BhG 8.18); another eternal unmanifest beyond it is the Imperishable (8.20); worshipped by some (12.1–5); in the Mokṣadharma the field, prakṛti (12.294.38).
'The unmanifest' (Kaṭha 1.3.11), which the sūtras deny to be Sāṃkhya's pradhāna (BS 1.4.1); Brahman is also called unmanifest (3.2.23).
A name of māyā, the unmanifest power of the Lord (VC 108).

notes: Whether this is the Sāṃkhya pradhāna is debated (Brahma Sūtra 1.4.1).

definitions.definition: The second-stage ascetic who hides his Pāśupata sign while his conduct is manifest.
The second stage, in which birth and sign are hidden and the ascetic courts dishonour among people.
A property that occurs in a locus only in part (e.g. monkey-contact in a tree), coexisting with its own absence — a test case for definitions of pervasion.
'This self is Brahman' (Māṇḍūkya 2): the practice sentence (abhyāsa-vākya), mahāvākya of the Atharvaveda and of Jyotirmaṭh.
The temple (built by another) where the first-stage practitioner lives; the Ratnaṭīkā says it stands for the teacher.

notes: Homonym of the Buddhist technical term āyatana (sense-base).

definitions.definition: Beings (bodies) not born from wombs exist, also on the evidence of the Veda (VS 4.2.9 C).
Rites and hymns for long life (AVŚ 8.1–2; VS 3.62).
Souls bound in saṃsāra by beginningless karma, their knowledge contracted.
A pseudo-reason whose probandum's absence is known by another means of knowledge ('fire is not hot').
Sublation: the cancellation of a cognition by a later one that shows its object never was as it appeared (the snake by the rope-cognition); the criterion of the three levels of reality.
The lapse of transferred details that serve no purpose in the ectype, e.g. husking for gold pieces (MS 10.1.1–2).
A later cognition that the object is otherwise, which (with knowledge of a causal defect) alone sets aside a cognition's validity.
The first five limbs; even the inner three are outer relative to seedless samādhi (3.8).
The external power, māyā, which produces the material world and covers the souls turned away from the Lord.
External worship of the deity in liṅga, image, maṇḍala or fire.
Second kind: triple staff, ochre, eight mouthfuls from many houses.
An alternative verse to the Raudrī Gāyatrī for expiation and recitation (usually taken as the Aghora mantra).
The ten capacities, operating in the present and presenting objects to the three internal ones (SK 33).
Devotion to the teacher, clarity of mind, conquest of opposites, merit and vigilance.
Food set out daily for beings (bhūtayajña) (ŚB 11.5.6.2); offerings 'not into fire' (ĀśGS 1.1.2).

Bondage comes from error (SK 44) and belongs to prakṛti, which binds herself by seven forms (SK 62–63); it is threefold — to prakṛti, to the modifications, and through gifts (Tattvasamāsa and Kramadīpikā).
The self's threefold connection with the world: the body (seat of experience), the senses (its instruments) and the objects (what is experienced) (Śāstradīpikā).
The three locks — root, abdominal, throat.

The hidden correspondence the Brāhmaṇas establish between an element of the rite, the cosmos and the person (e.g. the bricks of the altar = the days and nights of the year = the joints of Prajāpati); knowing the bandhu is what makes the rite effective.
The strewn grass on which the gods are invited to sit.
Allama's Kannada word for the void — open space without enclosure — in which the devotee, the liṅga and the world disappear.

equivalents.note: Kannada and Sanskrit words used side by side for the void in Allama's vacanas

definitions.definition: The enigmatic, paradoxical vacanas (beḍagina vacana) especially of Allama Prabhu.
The auspicious, prayed for in intention, hearing and seeing (RV 1.89.1, 1.89.8).
The six excellences whose possessor is Bhagavat: aiśvarya, vīrya, yaśas, śrī, jñāna, vairāgya.
Partial implication: the mode by which 'that' and 'thou' are understood as their common consciousness, dropping the opposed features, as in 'this is that Devadatta'.
