equivalents.note: the Rāma Gītā names it bhāga-lakṣaṇā after rejecting jahatī and ajahatī; later Advaita manuals call the same jahad-ajahal-lakṣaṇā

definitions.definition: Object of a meditation on the self, reported by Yāmuna as the Kāpāla means to nirvāṇa (restricted; opponent's report).
The scriptural duties as the Lord's commands, which the surrendered still obey (ājñā), and further services allowed but not required (anujñā).
The Lord as possessing the six qualities (knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility, splendour) without limit.

literal: the one possessing the six excellences

definitions.definition: The one possessing the six excellences - lordship, valour, fame, fortune, knowledge and detachment - who knows the origin and end of beings, knowledge and ignorance; properly Vāsudeva; with Brahman and Paramātman one of three names of the non-dual reality.
The Lord (Bhagavān), speaker of the Gītā ('śrībhagavān uvāca') and object of the Bhāgavatas' devotion; the Pañcarātra's whole knower is 'the Lord himself' (12.337.63).
The Lord as possessor of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya).
A devotee of the Lord; the Bhāgavata Purāṇa; devotees are themselves tīrthas (BhP 1.13.10).
A worshipper of Bhagavat (Vāsudeva); the Nārāyaṇīya says Sāṃkhyas together with Bhāgavatas enter Saṃkarṣaṇa on the path of liberation (12.332.16).
A follower of the Pāñcarātra; opponents held the Bhāgavatas/Sātvatas to be a low temple-serving class, Yāmuna that they are brahmins so named for a quality.
Offence against the Lord's devotees, including judging them by birth — graver than offence against the Lord.
The practices of devotion to Bhagavān, to be undertaken from childhood (BhP 7.6.1).
Livelihood of the first and third stages - whatever falls into the bowl.
The deity of the Kāpālikas in hostile portraits (Mahābhairava worshipped with liquor and alleged human offerings); the skull-bearing form of Śiva.
The supreme Śiva as the Trika names him; his true form is indescribable fullness identical with the Goddess, not the forms with parts described for meditation (VBT 7-16).
In the Śiva Sūtra the upsurge of awareness (udyama) is Bhairava (1.5).
The Atharvaveda's healing rites and hymns against fever, consumption, jaundice, leprosy, worms and demons.
Performance of devotional practice under a guru — the third stage.
The first sthala: one in whom devotion to Śiva has arisen; its dharma is taught in fifteen sub-sthalas (SSM 5.26–30).
One devoted to the Lord; the four kinds of devotee (BhG 7.16) and the devotee dear to him (12.13–20); 'my devotee never perishes' (9.31).

Firm love for Viṣṇu exceeding all other love, preceded by knowledge of his greatness; the sole means of liberation, to which all other practices are subsidiary, and itself eternal bliss in liberation.
Devotion to the Lord, by which he is known, seen and entered (BhG 11.54); supreme devotion is attained by one who has become Brahman (18.54), and by devotion one knows him in truth (18.55).
One-pointed devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa, 'the one devoted solely, intent on Nārāyaṇa' (MBh 12.336).
Devotion: the natural, motiveless inclination of the senses and mind toward the Lord, greater than liberation; by it alone the Lord is attained; it purifies even outcastes.
Loving devotion to Rāma, the lamp without which knowledge does not shine and the cause of liberation; open to men, women and even animals.
Devotion to the Goddess, the easiest of the three paths, graded by the guṇas and culminating in supreme devotion.

Devotion to Śiva, ninefold (SSM 9.2–3), outer and inner (9.6–9), arising from grace and giving rise to grace (9.11–12); its presence, not birth, makes one a bhakta (9.4–5); in the six-bhakti scheme it rises from faith to samarasa.

Unmotivated, uninterrupted love and service directed to the Lord, the highest dharma (BhP 1.2.6); graded by the guṇas and beyond them (3.29); ninefold in practice (7.5.23-24); the one means that 'wins' the Lord (11.14.20-21).
Meditation that has become love: knowledge in the form of supreme affection (prīti) for the Lord, the means to liberation prescribed by the Upaniṣads.
Devotion: 'to one who has the highest devotion to God and to his teacher as to God, these matters shine forth' (ŚU 6.23).

Devotion as the relish of identity with Śiva; for the one rich in devotion Śiva manifests without meditation or procedure (Śivastotrāvalī 1.1); the intense devotion of the dispassionate is Śaṅkara's power (VBT 121).
The relish of love for Kṛṣṇa, when the permanent emotion of love combines with its excitants, effects, bodily signs and transient emotions; the highest rasa.
Serving the Lord with unswerving devotion, by which one passes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for Brahman (BhG 14.26); the theme of ch. 12.
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva, the highest dharma (Nārāyaṇīya).
The yoga of devotion, fitting one in whom faith in the Lord's stories has arisen, who is neither disgusted with nor too attached to the world.
The loving meditation of the Upaniṣads, the direct means to the Lord, prepared by karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga and supported by the seven aids.
The principal act of prapatti: placing the burden of one's protection and its fruit on the Lord; often performed through a teacher.
The region south of the Himālaya and north of the ocean, the one land of action (karma-bhūmi), where the gods wish to be born.
The fullness of Bhairava's state (bharitākārā, VBT 15) and of the practitioner (VBT 24, 72, 117).
Ash, so called because it reproaches sins; bathing in ash is the supreme 'fire-bath' (SSM 7.4–5; 7.23–25).
Ash consecrated with the mantras, used for bathing thrice daily, lying on, re-bathing and initiation; the sign of the first stage.
The Atharvaśiras identifies all the elements with ash: 'fire is ash ... all this is ash'.
The ash of a cremation, smeared by a Kāpālika (Sattasaī) and listed by Yāmuna among the six Kāpāla insignia.
Sacred ash worn by Śaivas (often as the tripuṇḍra), praised in the Śiva Purāṇa.
Sacred ash from the sacred fire, smeared on all the limbs in the Pāśupata yoga.
Ash used in the Virajā initiation (Śiva Gītā).
Tirunīṟu, the sacred ash: mantra, medicine and the mark of Śiva's devotee.

notes: Also: vibhūti

definitions.definition: Sacred ash, prepared with mantras; worn in the pāśupata vow and the tripuṇḍra.
Bathing the body in consecrated ash at the three junctures of the day.

The eight dispositions of buddhi — virtue, knowledge, dispassion, power and their opposites (SK 23) — innate, natural or acquired (SK 43), which perfume the subtle body (SK 40) and by seven of which prakṛti binds herself (SK 63).
A name of Rudra, paired with Śarva (AVŚ 11.2).
Emotion: the stage after attachment in Rūpa's sequence, pure sattva that softens the heart; in the Ujjvalanīlamaṇi also the name of mahābhāva's threshold.
Devotion as emotion: the first sprouting of love, a ray of the sun of prema that softens the heart.
The state of the bodiless and those merged in prakṛti, which has becoming as its cause (1.19); Vijñānabhikṣu glosses bhava as birth.

literal: the liṅga of feeling / of pure being

definitions.definition: The liṅga in which feeling (bhāva) itself dissolves, grasped by devotion and worshipped with flowers of feeling, superior to liṅgas of clay or stone (SSM 15.37–44); in the vacana triad iṣṭa–prāṇa–bhāva the third, beyond form.

notes: SSM 6.49–50 names the third liṅga of the triad tṛptiliṅga.

definitions.definition: Cultivation: of the meaning of the praṇava (1.28), of the four attitudes (1.33), of the opposites of harmful thoughts (2.33); Vyāsa: equanimity toward the wicked is not a cultivation (YBh 3.23).

The operation of the one who brings about, expressed by the verbal suffix: verbal (śābdī) bhāvanā — the prompting power of the injunctive — and objective (ārthī) bhāvanā — the person's activity toward the result; each expects what (sādhya), by what (karaṇa) and how (itikartavyatā).
VP 6.7.48-51: the three contemplations of beings - of Brahman, of action, and of both.
The impression produced by experience that causes memory; resides only in the self (Tarkasaṅgraha).

notes: Homonym: in Buddhist and yoga contexts bhāvanā means cultivation / meditation.

definitions.definition: Ignorance as a positive entity (not a mere absence of knowledge), held by the Vivaraṇa line and later Advaita, proved by the experience 'I am ignorant'; rejected as un-Śaṅkaran by Satchidanandendra (recent).
A non-initiate or one averse to the conduct of the path; the SSM bids the devotee refuse goods sent by bhavis (9.30–32).
Real difference, which is the very nature (svarūpa) of each thing, grasped together with the thing itself; not a separate negation (anyonyābhāva). Fivefold and eternal between God, souls and matter.
Difference-and-non-difference: Brahman is at once one with and different from souls and world (one as cause, many as effect).
Natural difference-and-non-difference of cit and acit from Brahman, like snake and coils.
Held to be inconceivable (acintya) in the relation of the Lord and his powers.
A remedy — plants, waters, amulets and spells; Rudra has a thousand (RV 7.46.3); 'the waters are the remedy for all' (10.137.6).
Food begged by the renouncer; five kinds; better than unsolicited food.
Living on alms, the mendicant's life (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22; cf. MuU 1.2.11).
One who lives on alms; four kinds in the Bhikṣuka Upaniṣad.
Experience, which buddhi accomplishes for puruṣa (SK 37); with liberation, one of the two purposes for which prakṛti acts (commentaries on SK 21).

Experience: a cognition that fails to distinguish sattva and puruṣa (3.35); determining the guṇas as desired or undesired without discrimination (YBh 2.18); one of the two purposes of the seen (2.18).
The freed soul's equality with Brahman in the enjoyment of bliss, not in cosmic function.
The regions other than Bhārata, where beings only enjoy the fruits of past deeds.
The soul at the stages of prasādi and prāṇaliṅgi, correlated with the subtle body and the prāṇaliṅga.
The body, as the locus in which the self experiences pleasure and pain.
Puruṣa as experiencer, one proof of its existence (SK 17); experience culminates in consciousness (SS 1.104).
The enjoyer: the self joined with body, senses and mind (KU 1.3.4); enjoyer, enjoyed and impeller as the threefold brahman (ŚU 1.12).
Erroneous vision: false knowledge (YBh 1.30).
Humility — the attitude of a servant toward Śiva and his devotees (dāsōhaṃ).
The twofold fruit that all four pādas of Śiva's scripture serve.
Plenitude: that in which one sees, hears and understands nothing else; it is happiness and immortal, established in its own greatness (ChU 7.23-24).
A stage of knowledge (seven) or of ignorance (seven); also the four stages of yoga.
From saṃyama on the five forms of the elements (3.44).
The fourteenfold creation of beings: eight divine, five animal, one human (SK 53; Tattvasamāsa 18).
Scriptures of the western stream (Sadyojāta) for controlling and expelling spirits.
Ahaṃkāra in its tāmasa aspect, from which the subtle elements proceed (SK 25).
Elemental space, extended in the ten directions, the support of wind and clouds.
An arthavāda neither contradicted nor already established by another means (e.g. 'Indra raised the thunderbolt against Vṛtra').
The ritual-meditative dissolution of the body's elements into their sources and the re-creation of a pure, divine body before worship (the Kāmika's 'self-purification' corresponds in function).
Purification of the elements performed before worship of Bhagavān.
Performed by the tantri in the preliminary sequence of Kerala worship.
Seed-waking: the first pure, nameless stirring of consciousness, the seed of the future names 'jīva' and the like.
God as the original of which the soul is the reflection; the Lord in one's heart contemplated as 'you are the bimba, I am the reflection'.
The prototype or original of a reflection; in the Vivaraṇa, Īśvara/Brahman as the original of which the jīva is the reflection.
The point of Oṃ; the seed-essence (white and red) whose retention the haṭha passages seek; identified with mind.
The point arising from Nāda in the Śāradātilaka's account of emanation.
The point of light seen or meditated (VBT 36-37) and a subtle phase of a mantra's utterance (VBT 42, 90).
Pure māyā (śuddha-māyā, mahāmāyā, kuṭilā): the pure material cause of the pure universe, of the bodies of pure beings and of sound; distinct from Śiva, who does not change.

notes: Contribution from U08; U31/U28 own bindu.

definitions.definition: The hour before dawn for waking and reflecting on dharma, artha and the meaning of the Veda (MDh 4.92).
The goal reached by one established in the brāhmī state even at death (BhG 2.72) and by sages free of faults, delighting in the welfare of beings, for whom it lies near on every side (5.24–26).

equivalents.note: the Gītā's compound shares the word nirvāṇa with Buddhist usage; whether and how the meanings relate is disputed and each tradition defines its own term

definitions.definition: The state of the yogin at peace who has become Brahman (BhG 5.24, 6.27); having become Brahman, serene, he attains supreme devotion (18.54); fitness for it (brahmabhūya) comes from devotion (14.26) and discipline (18.53).
Practice of Brahman: thinking of it, speaking of it, awakening one another to it and being wholly devoted to it.
The wheel of brahman, in which the goose (haṃsa) wanders (ŚU 1.6) and which God's greatness turns (6.1).
The Vedic student, praised in AVŚ 11.5 as quickening both worlds by fuel, girdle, toil and tapas.
Restraint of the generative organ with the senses guarded (YBh 2.30); when established, vigour is gained (2.38).
Vedic studentship, by which the debt to the seers is paid (TS 6.3.10.5); the student is withheld from Death if he brings fuel and begs daily (ŚB 11.3.3).
The student's stage in the teacher's house, with chastity, begging and service; temporary or lifelong (naiṣṭhika).

The life of a student of the Veda, celibacy: what people call sacrifice is really brahmacarya (ChU 8.5); the brahma-world belongs to those who find it by brahmacarya (ChU 8.4.3); preparatory year of austerity, celibacy and faith (PrU 1.2).
The vow of celibacy of the meditator (BhG 6.14) and of those desiring the Imperishable (8.11); bodily austerity (17.14); Sanatsujāta's four quarters of brahmacarya (MBh 5.44).

cross_language.note: In Pali the holy life in general

definitions.definition: The sin incurred by Bhairava/Śiva in cutting off Brahmā's head, whose penance - wandering with the skull - the Kāpālika vow imitates.
The desire to know Brahman, i.e. the inquiry into Brahman, with which the Brahma Sūtras open.
The inquiry into Brahman undertaken after acquiring the four means, not after the inquiry into ritual.

The world of brahman: reached by the path of the gods (BAU 6.2.15) and by brahmacarya (ChU 8.4-5); described with its lake, river, tree, city and palace (KauU 1.3-5; ChU 8.5.3); in BAU 4.3.32 the ocean-like non-dual seer 'is the world of brahman'.
The world of the conditioned Brahman (Hiraṇyagarbha), reached by meditators on the qualified Brahman, where they are liberated at the end of the cycle.

In the Ṛgveda, the potent sacred formulation or prayer and the power in it (Bṛhaspati/Brahmaṇaspati is its lord); in the Atharvaveda and Yajurveda, the highest principle: 'that is brahman' (VS 32.1), 'homage to the highest Brahman' (AVŚ 10.8.1), 'those who know Brahman in man know the Supreme' (10.7.17), Brahman entered the golden city of the body (10.2.33).

The ultimate ground: that from which beings arise, by which they live and into which they go (TU 3.1.1); being, one without a second (ChU 6.2.1); truth, knowledge, infinite (TU 2.1.1); understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28); described also by negation (BAU 2.3.6). Also the name of the formula or sacred word in older usage.
That from which the origin, sustenance and dissolution of the world proceed, known from the Upaniṣads (BS 1.1.2–4).
The one reality without a second: existence–consciousness–bliss, attributeless (nirguṇa) in itself, identical with the inner self; associated with māyā it is Īśvara, the world-cause.

In Dvaita the word applies primarily to Viṣṇu alone, 'full' (pūrṇa) in qualities; defined as that from which come creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, knowledge, ignorance, bondage and release.
In the Brāhmaṇas: the sacred formulation and the Veda; also the first principle — 'in the beginning this was Brahman' (ŚB 11.2.3.1), 'Brahman the self-existent' (ŚB 10.6.5.9; 13.7.1.1; GB 1.1.1).
The supreme reached by self-knowledge and seeing the self in all (MDh 12.125); 'the one syllable is the supreme Brahman' (VDh 10.5).

The imperishable supreme (BhG 8.3), beginningless, neither being nor non-being (13.12), with hands and feet everywhere (13.13); also the Veda from which ritual action arises (3.15) and the prakṛti called 'great Brahman', the Lord's womb (14.3); 'na mama' is the eternal Brahman (MBh 12.13.4).
In the Purāṇas the supreme reality, identified with Viṣṇu (VP), Śiva (ŚiP), or the Goddess (DBhP); one of three names of non-dual knowledge (BhP 1.2.11).
The supreme reality, Nārāyaṇa, great in essence and qualities and making others great; qualified (saviśeṣa) by souls and matter, never an attributeless consciousness.
The liṅga itself, so named for its vastness and expanding (SSM 6.36–38); the liṅga of light by whose light all shines (12.38–41).
U04 usage: the one reality realized as 'so'ham'; the soundless beyond nāda; the goal of renunciation; named as Nārāyaṇa, Śiva, Rāma or the Goddess in the sectarian Upaniṣads.

cross_language.note: used in Pali mostly for the deity Brahmā or as 'excellent'

notes: U01 contribution: the Saṃhitā senses. The Upaniṣadic and Vedānta definitions are contributed by other units.

equivalents.note: Advaita holds Brahman and the inner self identical; other Vedānta schools deny strict identity.

definitions.definition: The priest who oversees the whole rite in silence and repairs its faults; Vāc makes whom she loves a brahmán (RV 10.125.5).

notes: The Atharvavedic tradition claims this office for Atharvavedins (dsp:atharvaveda-status).

definitions.definition: Whatever in the Veda is not mantra (MS 2.1.33): the injunctions, arthavādas and the like.
The prose portion of the Veda that enjoins rites and explains them; 'Veda is the name for mantra and brāhmaṇa' (ĀpŚS 24.1.31–32).

notes: The social class 'brāhmaṇa' is under trm:varna.

definitions.definition: The cosmic egg within which the fourteen worlds lie, enclosed by sheaths of the elements; broken up in the elemental dissolution.
Established in Brahman: having direct knowledge of the self, the second qualification of the teacher.
The opening at the crown; seat of the state beyond the fourth; exit of the breath that does not return.
The opening at the crown through which the yogin departs.
'Relation with Brahman': the initiation in which the disciple dedicates body, senses, mind, family and wealth to Kṛṣṇa, removing the five kinds of faults (Siddhāntarahasya).
The women named in the Bṛhaddevatā as speakers of Vedic verses.
Knowledge of brahman, 'the foundation of all knowledge', taught by Brahmā to Atharvan (MuU 1.1.1); to be taught only to those who performed the head-vow (MuU 3.2.10).
The state of the one of steady wisdom, attaining which one is not deluded (BhG 2.72).
The ritual exchange of riddles on cosmic matters (VS 23.9–12); RV 1.164 is composed in this manner.
A formal verbal contest on the hidden meaning of the rite and the cosmos, as between Yājñavalkya and Śākalya (ŚB 11.6.3) or Uddālaka and Svaidāyana (ŚB 11.4.1).
Lord of sacred speech (brahmaṇaspati), who smelted the worlds like a smith (RV 10.72.2) and is addressed in the hymn on knowledge (10.71).
The other principal sāman of the soma rite, paired with the rathantara (AVŚ 15.3).
In Mādhva usage the tomb-shrine of an ascetic saint, where the tradition holds the saint to remain present (e.g. Rāghavendra at Mantrālaya, Vyāsatīrtha at Nava Brindāvana).

literal: one wishing to enjoy / one wishing to be liberated

definitions.definition: The two orientations of Mantramārga initiates: seeking powers and enjoyments in the higher worlds, or seeking liberation; the Mantramārga caters for both.
In the Vasiṣṭha–Karāla dialogue, the twenty-sixth, the ever-awakened (MBh 12.296.7, 12.296.11).

notes: U05's definition (the epic Sāṃkhya usage); the Buddhist sense is defined by the Buddhist units.

definitions.definition: Not different from apprehension and knowledge (NS 1.1.15); a non-eternal quality of the self, not an eternal inner instrument (against Sāṃkhya, NS 3.2.1–9).
The cause of all usage; memory or experience (Tarkasaṅgraha).

The determining faculty (adhyavasāya, SK 23), whose sāttvika form is virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power and whose tāmasa form is their opposite; the door-keeper among the instruments (SK 35), which accomplishes all experience for puruṣa and discriminates puruṣa from pradhāna (SK 37).
The instrument of cognition (the 'power of seeing') whose apparent identity with the seer is I-am-ness (YBh 2.6); neither the same as the puruṣa nor wholly different (YBh 2.20).
The understanding, higher than mind (BhG 3.42); resolute and one in the yogin (2.41); its destruction follows loss of memory (2.63); threefold by the guṇas (18.29–32).
Intellect: the inner organ as deciding; the seat of the reflected consciousness and of the ego's agency.
Intellect: the charioteer (KU 1.3.3); higher than mind, below the great self (KU 1.3.10); it does not stir in the highest state (KU 2.3.10).

notes: Distinct from the Sāṃkhya-Yoga buddhi (mahat), a principle of prakṛti.

definitions.definition: Action guided by the resolute understanding that is free from attachment to fruits (BhG 2.49–50); the Lord gives it to his loving devotees (10.10) and Arjuna is told to resort to it (18.57).
Ear, skin, eye, tongue and nose (SK 26), whose function is mere awareness (ālocana) of sound and the rest (SK 28); later called jñānendriya.
The twenty-fifth as unawakened yet awakening (MBh 12.294.43; 12.296.3–10).
Consciousness as the self (Śiva Sūtra 1.1); Kṣemarāja: the absolute freedom of knowing and doing.
The guru within the heart: the Lord as Paramātman guiding from within.
A centre of the subtle body; six (or nine) in the Yoga Upaniṣads; also the Śrīcakra.
Centres through which the power rises (VBT 29); the Netratantra names six wheels, sixteen supports, three targets and five voids (Netra 7.1).
The image for the knower's continued embodiment by residual momentum (SK 67; SS 3.83).
The litany of petitions 'and … for me' (TS 4.7; VS 18).
The wondering relish of consciousness in itself; in the Śiva Sūtra 'wonder' marks the stages of yoga (1.12).
Kālī's name after slaying Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (DM 7).
The penance in which food follows the waning and waxing moon (MDh 11.216) — restricted content.
Bhagavad Gītā 18.66, read as the Lord's command to surrender to him alone, with the promise of freedom from all sins.
A school of Vedic study and ritual practice, often coextensive with a śākhā and its sūtras.
The series of acts from ash-bathing to feigned folly; threefold as gift, worship and austerity; twofold as vows and doors; the second means to the gains.
Conduct: the first of the four pādas (and a section of each Āgama) — rules of life and service.
Cariyai: temple service — cleaning, lamps, garlands, singing — the servant's path (dāsa-mārga), leading to sālokya.
The sixty-four Bhairava tantras in eight groups of eight (Śrīkaṇṭhīya).
The sixty-four tantras 'of the Mothers' named in the Vāmakeśvara, by which Paśupati 'beguiled the world' before revealing the Goddess's own tantra (Saundaryalaharī 31).
The four verses spoken by the Lord to Brahmā (BhP 2.9.32-35), held to be the seed of the whole Bhāgavata.
The fourfold order created by the Lord according to the division of guṇas and actions (BhG 4.13).
The true or perfect reality — the Real, Śiva; in the Kuṟaḷ the reality to be seen for birth to end.
Sentient dependent beings: Lakṣmī (eternally untouched by sorrow) and all souls, divided by their relation to sorrow and their fitness.
Puruṣa is conscious; the manifest and unmanifest are unconscious (acetana) (SK 11); the unconscious liṅga appears conscious through conjunction (SK 20).
Countering a statement by supposing an alternative meaning; verbal, generalizing and figurative (NS 1.2.10–17).
Vedic metre; the metres came from the Puruṣa sacrifice (RV 10.90.9).

Metre, the 'feet' of the Veda (PŚ 41); so called because the gods covered (chad) themselves with the metres against death (ChU 1.4.2). In Pāṇini, also the Vedic language as opposed to ordinary speech.
The fourth stage, ending in the cutting [of bonds], in the cremation ground.
The semblance or reflection of consciousness in the intellect, which makes the inner organ appear conscious; together with the kūṭastha it constitutes the jīva.
The space of consciousness: the knower within and without all beings that reveals existence; mind-space and elemental space arise from it.
'The space of consciousness': Chidambaram (Tillai), where Śiva dances in the 'small hall' (ciṟṟampalam); also the heart-space.
The bliss of consciousness gained by unfolding the centre, which, made firm, is liberation in life (PH 16-17).
Sentient reality: the individual souls, eternal, atomic knowers, bound, freed or eternally free; one of the three realities.
Consciousness: self-luminous awareness, the nature of the self and of Brahman, never an object.
The conscious reality: the souls, one of the three realities.
Śiva's power of consciousness, inseparable from him, identified with Umā and with the supreme ether; the world subsists in it subtly.
Consciousness as free power, the cause of the universe (PH 1); contracted, it is the individual and the mind (PH 4-5); its essence is reflexive awareness (ĪPK 1.5.13).
The puruṣa as the power of consciousness: unchanging, not passing over into objects, pure and infinite (YBh 1.2); kaivalya is its establishment in its own form (4.34).
Vācaspati's name for puruṣa as consciousness, to which suffering is disagreeable (on SK 1, 5).
Yama's recorder of the deeds of beings, consulted at judgment.

literal: mind; that which is conscious (as if)

definitions.definition: The mind, a product of prakṛti made of the three guṇas, whose activities are to be stilled; it is seen, not self-luminous, and exists for the sake of the puruṣa; one, having many objects, and enduring (YBh 1.32). Commentators gloss it as the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

Thought: a rung above intention in Sanatkumāra's ladder (ChU 7.5); with whatever thought one has one enters breath at death (PrU 3.10); 'the mind alone is saṃsāra' (cittam eva hi saṃsāraḥ, MaiU 6.34).
The inner organ as remembering and reflecting (in the fourfold Advaita division); in general usage, mind.
Consciousness descended and contracted by the knowable (PH 5); turned inward, it becomes consciousness again (PH 13).
The bound self is the mind (Śiva Sūtra 3.1); the mind is mantra (2.1).

equivalents.note: Nāgeśa glosses citta as antaḥkaraṇa; Yoga uses citta for the whole inner organ (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas together) rather than naming its parts.

definitions.definition: The five levels of the mind — scattered, stupefied, distracted, one-pointed, stilled (YBh 1.1).
The clearing of the mind that results from the four attitudes; the clear mind becomes one-pointed (1.33, YBh 1.33).

cross_language.note: Buddhist 'serenity/confidence of mind'

definitions.definition: Purification of the mind, the proper result of selfless action, which makes one fit for knowledge.
The name of the nine obstacles (1.30); called impurities of yoga and adversaries of yoga (YBh 1.30).
The space of mind: the creator pervading all through its conceiving.
Śiva as the auspicious absolute (neuter), identified with love in Tirumantiram 270.

The statement that impels to action (Śabara); the injunction, which alone makes known dharma, including what is future, subtle or remote. Śabara on MS 2.1.5 also uses 'codanā' for the apūrva the injunction makes known.

equivalents.note: codanā is the older (sūtra/bhāṣya) word; vidhi is the manual term, which also names one of the five kinds of Vedic sentence

definitions.definition: The fifth state of the afflictions, in one whose affliction-seeds are burnt by reflection, who is 'skilled' and in the last body (YBh 2.4); burnt-seed impressions give rise to no cognitions (4.28, YBh 4.28).
The small (space): 'in this city of brahman is a small lotus-dwelling, within it a small space; what is within that is to be sought' (ChU 8.1.1).
The small space in the lotus of the heart (Chāndogya 8.1), identified with Śiva as the supreme ether and the seat of meditation.

equivalents.note: the dahara is the space within the heart, not the heart itself

definitions.definition: Fate: in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha nothing but one's own former effort (prāk-pauruṣa); a name given to the fruit of one's deeds, without form, act or power of its own; relying on it is delusion.
The divine or fated factor, the fifth cause of action (BhG 18.14); which does not bear fruit without human effort, as a seed without a field (MBh 13.6.7).
The set of virtues — fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in knowledge and yoga, non-harm, truth, compassion and the rest — that leads to liberation (BhG 16.1–3, 16.5).
Skill and effective will; Vasiṣṭha pleads that his fault was 'not my own will (dakṣa)' (RV 7.86.6); Dakṣa is also the god born of Aditi (10.72.4).
The sacrificial fee and gift to the priests; the givers of gifts stand high in heaven and partake of immortality (RV 10.107.2).
The gift to the officiating priests, the 'human gods', as oblations go to the gods (ŚB 2.2.2.6); it does not reach the world attained by knowledge (ŚB 10.5.4.16).
The southern fire, associated with the fathers and protection.
Self-restraint, a mark of the divine endowment (BhG 16.1) and one of the three 'horses of Brahman' (MBh 11.7.19); taught by the Haṃsa (12.288).
Self-control: restraining the outer organs and turning them back to their sources.
Self-restraint: the gods' 'da' (BAU 5.2); among the virtues of BAU 4.4.23 (dānta); foundation of the upaniṣad with austerity and work (Kena 4.8).
Giving of wealth and food; the giver's wealth does not waste away, and 'who eats alone has only sin' (RV 10.117).
Giving, sāttvic when given because it ought to be given, to one who makes no return, at the right place and time to a worthy recipient (BhG 17.20).
Religious giving, especially to brahmins; at death the gifts (cow, land, sesame etc.) ease the road of the dead.
Giving: the humans' 'da' (BAU 5.2); 'give with faith' (TU 1.11.3); a priestly gift of the life-sacrifice (ChU 3.17.4).

The accomplishment of receiving knowledge from the venerable after serving them with shelter, medicine, staff, water-pot, food and clothing (Gauḍapāda on SK 51); Vācaspati is recalled as deriving it from the root 'dai' (to purify), the purity of discriminative knowledge (low confidence).
Punishment, which rules and protects all creatures and is itself dharma (MDh 7.18).
The renouncer's staff, of bamboo; never to be left more than three arrow-shots away (Sannyāsa); or the staff of knowledge.
The science of rule by the rod, composed by Brahmā when the first age declined (MBh 12.59); one of the three sciences sustaining the world (3.149.31–33).
The vividness that perfected meditation attains, equal to direct perception of the Lord.

literal: having the form of direct seeing

definitions.definition: The servant's path, corresponding to caryā and exemplified by Appar.
The Bhāgavata's ten marks of a (great) Purāṇa, given in two different lists (BhP 2.10.1; 12.7.9-10); the tenth, āśraya/apāśraya, is the support for whose sake the other nine are told.
'The tenth (man)': illustration of the self overlooked by the counter and recognized immediately through the words 'you are the tenth'.

(1) The devotee's self-understanding as servant of Śiva and his devotees, which Basava asks for in place of 'I am He'; (2) the giving of the fruits of one's work (kāyaka) to the jaṅgamas and the community, and in later usage free communal feeding.

equivalents.note: dāsōha includes service but also names the servant-stance and the sharing of earned wealth

definitions.definition: The attitude and practice of being the Lord's servant, the seventh form of devotion.
The rasa of servitude: love for Kṛṣṇa as master, with a sense of his superiority.
Agitation of mind from thwarted desire (YBh 1.31).
Compassion: the asuras' 'da' — be compassionate (dayadhvam) (BAU 5.2.3).
The Lord's compassion, personified by Deśika as a goddess in the Dayāśataka; the schools define it differently.
The self as dweller in the body, which passes through bodily stages and into new bodies as one changes clothes (BhG 2.13, 2.22, 2.30); bound in the body by the guṇas (14.5).
The final ending of embodiment that is release (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
The supports by whose power the practitioner grows: teacher, people, cave, cremation ground, Rudra.
A god; thirty-three in heaven, earth and waters (RV 1.139.11) or 3,339 (3.9.9).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan daēva (demon).

definitions.definition: The third gain, sought in the stage of conquest.

That to which an offering is directed as named in the injunction or mantra; subordinate to the sacrificial act, which alone produces the fruit (MS 9.1.9); not established as embodied or eating the offering (Śabara).
The deity addressed by a verse, recorded with its seer and metre in the Anukramaṇīs; in the person 'all deities dwell as cows in a stall' (AVŚ 11.8.32).
The bright path of fire, light, day, the bright fortnight and the northern course, by which knowers of Brahman go to Brahman and do not return (BhG 8.24).
The path of the gods, distinct from death's own path (RV 10.18.1) and from the fathers' (10.88.15).

The path of the gods: through flame, day, the waxing fortnight, the northern course, the year (or the gods' world), the sun, the moon and lightning, where a non-human person leads to brahman; those who go by it do not return (ChU 4.15.5, 5.10.1-2; BAU 6.2.15; PrU 1.10; KauU 1.3).
The path of the gods, beginning with light (arcis), by which meditators go to Brahman/the Brahma-world without return (BS 4.3.1).

notes: U05's contribution (the Gītā's form of the Upaniṣadic doctrine).

definitions.definition: Fixing the mind on a support - the Lord's form (VP, BhP) or bodily places and the subtle elements (MkP).
Concentration: binding the mind to a place (3.1) — navel, heart-lotus, light in the head, tip of the nose or tongue, or an external object (YBh 3.1).
Fixation of the mind, which burns away sin (MDh 6.72).
Holding the mind in concentration: 'established in yogic concentration' at death (BhG 8.12); the concentrations of the Mokṣadharma's yoga (12.289).
Holding the mind in the heart.
Holding, concentration: yoga is the firm holding (dhāraṇā) of the senses (KU 2.3.11); fourth limb in MaiU 6.18.
Concentration; the five element-concentrations; holding mind in the Self.
Each of the 112 'teachings of the waveless state' of the Vijñāna Bhairava (v. 139); in the Mālinīvijayottara, concentrations on elements, subtle elements and senses (chs. 12-17).

The whole of right conduct — ritual, moral, social and legal — rooted in the Veda, smṛti, the practice of the good and self-approval (MDh 2.6); it protects when protected and alone follows one after death (MDh 8.15–17; 4.238–242); its tenfold mark is steadfastness, patience, self-control, not stealing, purity, sense-restraint, wisdom, learning, truth and absence of anger (MDh 6.92).
The merit that correct usage of words brings, for which grammar restricts usage (first vārttika).

The upholding order and right conduct: its decline occasions the Lord's descent (BhG 4.7); one's own dharma is better than another's (3.35); it is subtle (MBh 8.49) and its truth hidden (vulgate Yakṣapraśna); from it come artha and kāma (18.5.49); non-cruelty is its highest form (3.297.55).

A sāttvika disposition of buddhi (SK 23) leading to upward movement (SK 44), not to liberation; Gauḍapāda defines it by compassion, giving and the yamas and niyamas of the Pātañjala. With knowledge, virtue and the rest cease to act as causes (SK 67).

That from which prosperity and the highest good result (VS 1.1.2); a quality of the self produced by enjoined acts (Tarkasaṅgraha); the knowledge of the categories arises from dharma manifested by the Lord's command (Praśastapāda).

The beneficial object (artha) whose defining mark is Vedic injunction (codanā) — concretely the sacrifice and other enjoined acts, which join a person with the highest good; what is enjoined but harmful (e.g. the Śyena, whose aim is violence) is not dharma.
An object with a purpose, made known by the Veda (Arthasaṅgraha): the sacrifice and the like.

Dharma: created by brahman as the power of the ruling power, higher than all; dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); 'practise dharma' (TU 1.11); three branches of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); Naciketas asks for what is other than dharma and adharma (KU 1.2.14); one's own dharma rescues the elemental self (MaiU 4.3).

cross_language.note: cognate; the Buddhist senses are defined by the Buddhist units

definitions.definition: The inquiry into dharma through the investigation of Vedic sentences, undertaken after Vedic study and before returning from the teacher's house (MS 1.1.1 with Śabara).
The change of a property-bearer's manifest property (e.g. emergence giving way to stilling; lump to pot) (3.13).

Attributive consciousness: the soul's (and the Lord's) consciousness as a quality distinct from the self-luminous substrate; eternal, it contracts in bondage through karma and expands fully in liberation; it goes out to objects as a lamp's light.
The samādhi of one who, detached even from the highest reflection, has complete discriminative discernment and no other cognitions (4.29, YBh 4.29); from it afflictions and karma cease (4.30).

notes: The same compound names the tenth bodhisattva ground (dharmameghā bhūmi) in Mahāyāna; see brw:mahayana-yoga-dharmamegha.

definitions.definition: What upholds; an ordinance or foundation; the first sacrifices were 'the first dharmas' (RV 10.90.16 = 1.164.50); the dead go to heaven and earth 'according to dharman' (10.16.3).
The substrate that conforms to properties past, present and not yet determinable (3.14).
A verbal root, listed in the Dhātupāṭha (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.1: 'bhū and the rest are roots').

notes: Other senses (bodily tissue, element) belong to other units.

definitions.definition: The visionary thought or insight of the seer, which is 'yoked' (RV 5.81.1) and which Savitṛ is asked to impel (3.62.10).
The wise, steadfast one: chooses the good over the pleasant (KU 1.2.2); turns his sight inward (KU 2.1.1).
Steadfastness, threefold by the guṇas; the sāttvic holds mind, breath and senses by unswerving yoga (BhG 18.33–35).
The immovable principal image standing for Viṣṇu's partless form.

equivalents.note: common temple usage 'mūlabera'

definitions.definition: Unbroken remembrance of the Lord flowing like a stream of oil, the form that liberating meditation takes (from Chāndogya 7.26.2, 'dhruvā smṛtiḥ').
The audible noise (nāda) produced by effort, which manifests the eternal letters; its loudness increases, not the word (MS 1.1.17).
Sustained meditation on Viṣṇu with his qualities, according to one's fitness, which produces direct knowledge; not a mere subsidiary of hearing.
Meditation: the continuous flow of a single cognition on the place of concentration (3.2); the means of abandoning the afflictions' activities (2.11).
Meditation, which burns away the 'ungodly qualities' and lets one see the course of the inner self (MDh 6.72–73).
VP 6.7.91: one continuous flow of the form's awareness, desiring nothing else; ŚiP 7.2.39: with object and then without.
Meditation is the removal of passion, accomplished through the cessation of mental modifications (SS 3.30–31); meditation is mind without object (SS 6.25).

Meditation: a rung of the ladder (ChU 7.6); the 'yoga of meditation' by which the sages saw God's power (ŚU 1.3); the friction of meditation (ŚU 1.14); a limb in MaiU 6.18; one sees him 'meditating' (MuU 3.1.8).
Meditation with or without qualities; 'so'ham'; one-pointedness on consciousness.

cross_language.note: Buddhist absorption levels — broader and differently structured

definitions.definition: Meditation as taught in BhG 6.10–32 (a firm seat, erect posture, gaze on the nose-tip, mind fixed on the self or the Lord) and 18.52; in the Mokṣadharma a fourfold dhyāna-yoga (12.188).
One, all-pervading, eternal substance, cause of the notion 'this (is) from here' and of directions (VS 2.2.12 C).

That by which supreme knowledge is given (dī) and the bondage of fetters destroyed (kṣī) (SSM 15.7); in Vīraśaiva practice the liṅga-initiation, with bathing, the whispered five-syllable mantra and the giving of the liṅga into the disciple's hand (6.19–25); by it the duality of guru and disciple is removed (19.6–7).

The consecration that makes the sacrificer fit for the soma rite, with restraint, vigil and tapas; with tapas it is among the powers that uphold the earth (AVŚ 12.1.1) and was first undertaken by the seers (AVŚ 19.41.1).
The consecration of the sacrificer before a Soma rite, by which the priests 'make him an embryo again' (AB 1.3); he keeps vows and is reborn at the final bath.
The consecration for sacrifice counted as the twice-born's third birth (MDh 2.169).
Consecration of a tested brahmin with mantra-sanctified ash before the southern image, with the hearing of the mantra.
Initiation into Hari's worship and mantra by the ācārya (with the sipping of the Lord's foot-water and vows); those without it are called 'beasts among men'.

The rite performed on the soul — not on caste or body — by which the guru, empowered by Śiva's mantras, joins the soul to Śiva and destroys its bonds; it is the cause of the other means (ritual, knowledge, conduct).
Initiation into Bhagavān's mantras and worship, in Śrīvaiṣṇava usage centred on the five sacraments (pañcasaṃskāra).

Initiation, in many forms (TĀ 14-22); for one who knows the Heart, initiation needs no sesame and ghee (Parātrīśikā 25); Spanda calls identification with the meditated 'the initiation of nirvāṇa' (SK 2.7).
Initiation, so called because it gives divine knowledge and destroys sin; the guru gives the mantras (gopāla-mantra, kāma-gāyatrī), which are not published.
Two initiations: the refuge mantra (nāma-nivedana) and the brahmasambandha.

notes: The vacana and manual tradition speak of three modes (by touch, by mantra, by rite: vedhā, mantra, kriyā) — moderate confidence.

definitions.definition: Material (the threefold effect: disciple's and teacher's knowledge, the kalās such as darbha, ash, sandal, thread, flowers, incense, mantras, and the brahmin to be consecrated), time (forenoon), rite, image and teacher.
The divine eye given by Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna to see the universal form (BhG 11.8) and by Vyāsa to Sañjaya to see the war (MBh 6.2).
The 108 temples sung by the Āḻvārs (106 on earth, with the Milky Ocean and Vaikuṇṭha), where the Lord abides in his image form.
A year of the gods, equal to 360 human years (a human year is a day and night of the gods).
Divine madness: the highest state of mahābhāva in separation, with speech such as citra-jalpa, seen in Rādhā and in Caitanya's last years.
Characterized by impelling to activity (NS 1.1.18); three groups: attachment, aversion, delusion (NS 4.1.3).

notes: Homonym: in Āyurveda doṣa means the three humours.

definitions.definition: The Lord as relishing, out of motherly love, the very faults of those who take refuge in him.

literal: one for whom faults are enjoyable

definitions.definition: The seer, the puruṣa: seeing alone, pure, seeing by conforming to cognitions (2.20); the witness of the buddhi (YBh 2.17); its conjunction with the seen is the cause of suffering (2.17).
Puruṣa as seer (SK 19), who sees prakṛti like a spectator once knowledge arises (SK 65).
Cause of the first flowing; natural in water, occasioned (by fire) in earth (ghee) and fire (gold).
What possesses motion and qualities and is an inherent cause (VS 1.1.14 C); nine (VS 1.1.4 C).
Firm conception or imagining, the second seed of the mind, identified with vāsanā.
The liberated's power of knowing: seeing, hearing, thinking, knowing (all treatises) and omniscience.

equivalents.note: Kauṇḍinya calls the same power jñānaśakti (PABh 5.46)

definitions.definition: One who surrenders and waits until his begun karma is exhausted.
Perception, defined as determination concerning each object (SK 5); in the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, the cognition that, in contact, reflects its object's form (SS 1.89).

literal: to be experienced in the seen (present) birth

definitions.definition: Karma ripening in this life, e.g. from intense practice or grave harm (2.12, YBh 2.12).
A thing about which ordinary people and critical examiners agree (NS 1.1.25).
The doctrine that perception is creation: objects exist only while perceived, as in dream (Prakāśānanda).
The seen, the whole world of objects; the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha's teaching turns on the realization that the seen does not exist apart from consciousness.
The seen: of the nature of illumination, activity and inertia, consisting of elements and senses, for experience and liberation (2.18), existing for the seer's sake (2.21).
Wiping away of the seen: the mind's erasure of the world through the knowledge 'the seen does not exist', from which the bliss of nirvāṇa arises.
Deceit and injurious intent; wrongs against the gods (RV 7.86.5 'drugdhāni').

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan druj (the Lie).

definitions.definition: Pain, the first accompaniment of distraction, threefold — from oneself, other beings, the gods (1.31, YBh 1.31); for the discerning everything is suffering (2.15); future suffering is what is to be avoided (2.16).
Characterized by affliction (NS 1.1.21); twenty-one kinds (Vācaspati); its absolute cessation is liberation.
Of the self (bodily and mental), from beings and from the gods; also fivefold as womb, birth, ignorance, old age and death.
Liberation: twofold - the absolute cessation of all suffering, and the attainment of lordship consisting in the powers of knowing and acting; reached through the Lord's grace.
Yāmuna reports it as the absolute cessation of pain understood as the destruction of the soul's special qualities (opponent's report).

equivalents.note: the Pāśupata name for liberation; it adds the Lord's powers to cessation
Nyāya's apavarga is cessation only; the Pāśupatas insist theirs is more (SDS 6/3)

definitions.definition: The three kinds of suffering that prompt the inquiry (SK 1): internal, from other beings, and from the divine (named by the commentaries); their complete cessation is the supreme goal (SS 1.1).
A holy sound like a bull's bellow made by touching tongue-tip to palate; part of the offering.

notes: Also written huḍukkāra (SDS, Ratnaṭīkā) and dunduṃkāra (Sagar text).

definitions.definition: Texts other than and contrary to the true scriptures; Janārdana is not known through them; some are said to have been produced to delude.
The point twelve finger-breadths beyond (above or outside) the body where the breath ends and the mind is to be cast (VBT 28, 50-51).
Duality: 'where there is duality, as it were, one sees another' (BAU 2.4.14, 4.5.15).

The usual outside name for Madhva's Vedānta, stressing real difference; Madhva himself reads 'dvaita' in the Māṇḍūkya as what is 'known otherwise' (wrongly) and 'advaita' as the Lord who has no equal.
'Dual-non-dual': name of Nimbārka's Vedānta, synonymous with svābhāvika-bhedābheda.

equivalents.note: the school uses both names

definitions.definition: Pairs such as cold and heat, which no longer assail one who has mastered posture (2.48); bearing them is austerity (YBh 2.32).
The pairs such as heat and cold, pleasure and pain, from which one should be free (BhG 2.45, 5.3); the delusion of opposites born of desire and aversion (7.27).
The third strength; endurance of heat and cold and the like, as cows and deer endure them.
The third age, in which worship/service (paricaryā, arcana) is the principal means; in each Dvāpara a Vyāsa divides the Veda and condenses the Purāṇa.
The six feigned behaviours (snoring, trembling, limping, amorous gestures, senseless acts, senseless speech) that are 'doors' to the increase of merit and loss of demerit by producing dishonour.
The two-sentence mantra of surrender: in the first the soul takes refuge at the feet of Nārāyaṇa with Śrī; in the second it prays for service to the divine couple.
Aversion, which follows on pain (2.8).
A mark and special quality of the self; as a fault, one of the three groups (NS 4.1.3); 'aversion is anger' (Tarkasaṅgraha).
A member of the first three classes, born a second time by initiation (MDh 2.169–171; 10.4).
One of the seven concentric island-continents of Bhū-maṇḍala (Jambu, Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, Puṣkara), each ringed by an ocean.
The product of two atoms, still imperceptible; through dyads and so on the gross elements arise (Praśastapāda).
Heaven, paired with Earth.
The doctrine that there is only one jīva, other beings being appearances within its ignorance, as figures in a dream.
The aikya sub-stage in which, contemplating the universe as made of Śiva, one's self is the single vessel of Śiva (SSM 14.28–33).
Renouncer with a single staff; truly, 'one who bears the staff of knowledge'.
The eleventh lunar day of both fortnights, kept by fasting, with detailed rules for days overlapped by the tenth.
The eleventh lunar day of each fortnight, kept with fasting for Viṣṇu; so powerful by the Nārada's praise that Yama's realm was emptied.
The one-pointed mind, in which samprajñāta yoga occurs (YBh 1.1).
One-pointedness of mind, a mental property that rises as all-objectness dwindles (3.11–12); a fruit of purity (2.41).

cross_language.note: a jhāna factor

definitions.definition: The state in which the subsiding and arising cognitions are alike (3.12).
'The One Being the inspired call by many names' (RV 1.164.46).

equivalents.note: Both name the One of the speculative hymns; 1.164.46 speaks of the One named by the gods' names, 10.129 of That One before creation.

definitions.definition: The dharma of the ekāntins, the best and dear to Nārāyaṇa, equal to Sāṃkhya-yoga, by which one goes to the imperishable Hari (MBh 12.336.4, 12.336.69); sung by the Lord to Arjuna before the battle (12.336.8).
One devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, dwelling in the White Island or entering Vāsudeva directly without the intermediate goals (MBh 12.323.26; 12.336.3–4; 12.332.18).
Resting the mind on a single principle to counter the obstacles (1.32, YBh 1.32).
Oneness with the Lord (merging), the fifth kind of liberation, which pure devotees do not accept.

equivalents.note: later Vaiṣṇava lists name the fifth liberation sāyujya; the Bhāgavata verse says ekatva

definitions.definition: Being one sentence with another, by which arthavādas and subsidiary statements share the purport of an injunction (MS 1.2.7, 2.1.46).
The Vrātya become sole lord (AVŚ 15.1.6).
Name of the Veda-branch claimed as the root of the Pāñcarātra; Vedānta Deśika's Pāñcarātrarakṣā gives primary eligibility to the Ekāyanins.

notes: The Chāndogya (7.1.2) lists an 'ekāyana' among Nārada's studies; the identification is the tradition's.

definitions.definition: The SSM's elaboration of the path into 101 sthalas — 44 on the side of the soul (aṅga) and 57 on the side of the liṅga — from piṇḍa to jñānaśūnya (1.28–31; 15.1–3).
Sin as a burden or stain, one's own or inherited from the fathers, from which Varuṇa is asked to release (RV 7.86.5, 7.89.5).

The eight qualities of the Lord (Kuṟaḷ 9's 'eṇkuṇattāṉ'), glossed by Parimēlaḻakar from the Śaiva Āgamas: self-dependence, pure body, natural understanding, omniscience, natural freedom from bonds, boundless grace, infinite power, boundless bliss.
Read by Jain interpreters of the Kuṟaḷ as the eight qualities of a liberated Siddha (reported here from the dispute; U34 may refine).
Desire, pursuit: the three desires — for sons, for wealth and for worlds — which knowers of the self rise above to live as mendicants (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22).
The three desires — for wife/sons, wealth and worlds — risen above in renunciation.
A Sāmaveda song-book giving the verses transformed into melodies.
Śiva's attendants — the pramathas such as Reṇuka and Dāruka (SSM 2.25–27; 3.67–77) — and by extension the community of devotees whose defence is gaṇācāra.
A group of three syllables classified by its pattern of heavy and light, used to define metres (Piṅgala, ch. 1).

Defence of the faith and the devotees against insult and harm; the SSM bids the devotee protect liṅgas and devotees even at the cost of life and, on meeting a reviler of Śiva, to have him killed, curse him or leave (9.33–36).
Quality grasped by the nose; fragrant or not; in earth only.
The Vaikhānasa self-description: made Vaiṣṇavas before birth by the prenatal viṣṇubali rite, they need no further Vaiṣṇava initiation such as branding.
The western, household fire of the three śrauta fires.
Scriptures of the eastern stream for neutralising poison with Garuḍa mantras.
The seven secondary rasas: humour, wonder, heroism, compassion, anger, fear and disgust, appearing within devotion.
The metre of three eight-syllable lines, and the Sāvitrī verse in it (RV 3.62.10), repeated with the vyāhṛtis (VS 36.3).
A Vedic metre of 24 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
The most complex common recitation (ab ba abc cba abc, …), guarding the order of every word.
Second stage, in which breaths, mind and selves unite.
Scriptural texts (such as the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa and Subāla Upaniṣad) that teach the body–self relation and so reconcile the texts of difference and of non-difference.
Pot-space: space delimited by a pot, stock illustration of the jīva as the one self delimited by bodies (GK 3.3).
Singing of the Lord's qualities, according to the rules of music; a vocal act of the offering.
Kṛṣṇa's highest abode, where he plays eternally with his associates; the manifest Vraja on earth is non-different from it.
The women of Vraja whose love for Kṛṣṇa, in union and separation, is the Bhāgavata's model of devotion.
White clay from Dvārakā for Vaiṣṇava marks.
Asking the Lord to be one's protector; fourth limb of prapatti.
The grasping instruments, the senses (1.41); the first of the five forms of the senses mastered by saṃyama (3.47).
The grasper, the puruṣa (as it appears to the mind), one of the three objects of coalescence (1.41, YBh 1.41).
Objects to be grasped — gross and subtle elements, the world (1.41, YBh 1.41).
The correlated objects and subjects that make the universe manifold (PH 3).
The yogin's distinction is attentiveness to their relation (VBT 106).

literal: to be sung in the village

definitions.definition: The melodies sung in the village (public ritual).
One of three knots (of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra) pierced by kuṇḍalinī.
The householder, 'eldest' of the orders, supporting the others as air supports beings (MDh 3.77–78; 6.89–90).
Keeping the vow, knowledge and pure words (mantras) concealed.
The cave: the hidden place (in the heart) where the self or brahman is set (TU 2.1.1; KU 1.2.12, 1.2.20, 1.3.1; MuU 2.1.10).
The secret teaching: the ancient yoga (BhG 4.3), the royal secret (9.2), the most secret (15.20, 18.63–64), not to be told to the undisciplined or undevoted (18.67).

The three constituents of prakṛti — sattva, rajas, tamas — of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion, serving illumination, activity and restraint, and functioning by mutual domination, support, production and pairing (SK 12).
What resides in a substance, has no qualities and is not an independent cause of conjunction and disjunction (VS 1.1.15 C); twenty-four (Praśastapāda).
Strand: the nine-gated lotus is 'covered with three strands' (AVŚ 10.8.43).

The three strands born of prakṛti — sattva, rajas and tamas — which bind the embodied one (BhG 14.5), act upon one another as the true agents (3.27–28), and classify faith, food, austerity, giving, knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness (chs. 17–18).

The three constituents of the seen — sattva (illumination), rajas (activity), tamas (inertia) (2.18); their conflicting activity makes all suffering for the discerning (2.15); everything is a particular arrangement of them (4.13); at kaivalya they return to their source (4.34).
The three qualities of the self — sattva, rajas, tamas — determining destinies (MDh 12.24–51).

The three qualities belong to the intellect, not to the self; everything is classed by them with a fourth, attributeless class belonging to the Lord; one conquers rajas and tamas by sattva and sattva by desirelessness.
The three qualities of Prakṛti (sattva, rajas, tamas) by which devotion (BhP 3.29), Purāṇas (Matsya 53.68-69) and the measures of Oṃ (MkP 42.4) are classified.

Quality, strand: God's power hidden by its own guṇas (ŚU 1.3); the jīva is bound to the guṇas and has three guṇas (ŚU 5.7); tamas, rajas and sattva as successive states and as Rudra, Brahmā and Viṣṇu (MaiU 5.2).

cross_language.note: as used in Chinese Buddhist accounts of Sāṃkhya (Paramārtha, Kuiji); recalled, verify
as used in Tibetan doxographies (grub mtha'); recalled, verify

notes: Distinct from the Sāṃkhya sense (the three constituents of prakṛti).
alt_notes: The Sāṃkhya sense (three qualities) is contributed by other units; identifying the two is a later reading (see interpretation_log).

definitions.definition: Viṣṇu's possession of infinite auspicious qualities, each unlimited; the reason he is called 'great' (Brahman).

One who neither hates nor longs for the guṇas' effects, sits as if indifferent knowing that the guṇas act, is the same in pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour, and has renounced all undertakings (BhG 14.22–25); reached by unswerving devotion (14.26).

An arthavāda that conflicts with another means of knowledge and is taken figuratively (e.g. 'the sacrificial post is the sun'; 'the sacrificer is the grass-bundle') (MS 1.2.10; grounds listed at MS 1.4.23–28).

Teacher: the self is its own chief teacher; yet ignorance-bound persons need a knower of the principles to give knowledge; the avadhūta takes twenty-four teachers from nature; the guru is the helmsman of the human boat.
In the Guru Gītā: 'gu' is darkness, 'ru' its remover; the guru is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara and the supreme Brahman; the root of liberation is his grace.

Īśvara is the teacher (guru) even of the ancients, unlimited by time (1.26); devotion offers all actions to the supreme teacher (paramaguru, YBh 2.1); Vyāsa: in the stages of saṃyama 'yoga itself is the teacher' (YBh 3.6).

'Gu' is what is beyond the qualities and 'ru' what is beyond form; the guru gives that (SSM 15.8–9); Śiva stands present as the guru and the two are not to be distinguished (11.19–21); without devotion to the guru no devotion to Śiva arises (11.22–24).
'The teacher is the means' (Śiva Sūtra 2.6); from the teacher comes awakening to the wheel of letters (2.7).
The teacher who is learned in scripture and established in Brahman, through whom alone the knowledge is to be sought (MU 1.2.12); approached with humility, service and questioning.
The one who knows the nine groups and consecrates the disciple; a mere knower of texts without faith is a semblance of a teacher.
Teacher: 'he should go to a teacher learned in the Veda and established in brahman' (MuU 1.2.12); devotion to the teacher as to God (ŚU 6.23).

The teacher from whose grace the qualified disciple gains the supreme knowledge; the lineage runs from Nārāyaṇa and Vyāsa through Madhva and the maṭha pontiffs; devotion to the teacher as to God is enjoined.
The guru-principle, without knowing which sacrifice, vows and pilgrimage are fruitless; the guru as not other than the Self.
The first strength.
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the māheśvara stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
The lineage from the Lord and Śrī through Viṣvaksena, Nammāḻvār, Nāthamuni, Yāmuna and Rāmānuja, recited before study.
Approaching and surrendering to the guru as the means, for one unable to follow the other means.
Non-inherent cause of the first falling; in earth and water.
The swan seated in the bright, in men, in ṛta, in the sky (RV 4.40.5); in the Atharvaveda the swan rising from the waters that never lifts one foot is Prāṇa (AVŚ 11.4.21).

Goose, swan: the self or God as the goose seated in the bright (KU 2.2.2); the goose that wanders in the wheel (ŚU 1.6); flutters outward in the city of nine gates (ŚU 3.18); the one goose in the midst of the world (6.15).
The self moving with the breath (ha out, sa in), meditated as a bird and repeated naturally 21,600 times a day; also the third kind of renouncer.
The mantra the living being repeats with each breath, going out with sa and in with ha (VBT 155b).

equivalents.note: Haṃsa reversed is so'ham ('I am He'): the same breath-mantra read as identity.

definitions.definition: Third kind: one night in a village, five in a town; lunar fasts.
One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): The absence of the conjunction, the seer's kaivalya (2.25).
One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): Unwavering discriminative discernment (2.26); right seeing (YBh 2.15).
Name of Viṣṇu in the formula 'Hari is supreme over all' (Hari-sarvottama); controller of all, under whom all dependent reality stands.
The central tenet that Viṣṇu is supreme over all beings; the 'great purport' (mahātātparya) of all scripture.
Loud laughter ('a-ha-ha', aṭṭahāsa) offered to the Lord; a vocal act.
Haṭha-yoga: eight limbs with mudrās; in the Yogaśikhā, the union of ha (sun) and ṭha (moon).
The mansion-temple in which the Lord's form is served as a householder's child and lord, with its own music (havelī saṅgīt).
That which is offered into the fire.
The member that proves what is to be proved by similarity or dissimilarity to the example (NS 1.1.34–35).
A reason that only appears to be one; five in the sūtra: inconclusive, contradictory, prakaraṇasama, sādhyasama, kālātīta (NS 1.2.4).
Five in the Navya list: inconclusive, contradictory, counterbalanced, unestablished, sublated (Tarkasaṅgraha); defined generally in the Tattvacintāmaṇi's hetvābhāsa-sāmānya-nirukti.
One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): Suffering yet to come (2.16); saṃsāra full of suffering (YBh 2.15).

literal: cause of what is to be avoided

definitions.definition: One of the four parts of the śāstra, modelled on medicine (YBh 2.15): The conjunction of seer and seen (2.17).
Brahman's freedom from, and opposition to, every defect: ignorance, karma, change, suffering.

literal: opposed to all that is to be shunned

definitions.definition: Injury to living beings; meat cannot be had without it (MDh 5.48).
The humming sound 'hiṃ' preceding a sāman.
The Golden Germ that arose in the beginning as the one lord of what exists (RV 10.121.1).
In the Purāṇas the cosmic creator Brahmā as the first embodied being; in VP 6.7.51 the being whose contemplation is of both Brahman and action.
The cosmic subtle being: consciousness identified with the aggregate of subtle bodies (sūtrātman), collective counterpart of taijasa.
The golden germ, whom Rudra saw being born (ŚU 3.4, 4.12).

equivalents.note: The last verse of RV 10.121 answers the refrain with 'Prajāpati'; the Anukramaṇī names the deity Ka (Prajāpati).

definitions.definition: The channels called hitā, extending from the heart, fine as a hair split a thousandfold, into which the self slips in deep sleep (BAU 2.1.19, 4.3.20; KauU 4.19).
The pleasure-giving aspect of the internal power; its essence is prema and its fullest embodiment is Rādhā.
A regional custom discussed as an example of practices of some that are dharma for all (MS 1.3.15–23, per commentaries).
The priest who recites the Ṛgveda verses; Agni is the divine hotṛ (RV 1.1.1).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): cognate of Avestan zaotar.

definitions.definition: The heart as the place of inner seeing: the seers searched in the heart (RV 10.129.4); the light is set in the heart (6.9.6); the wise see with heart and mind (10.177.1); the mind is heart-seated (VS 34.6).
The Heart of the Supreme: consciousness as vibrancy and great being (ĪPK 1.5.14).
The Heart of Bhairava, the seed in which the universe lies like a tree in a banyan seed (Parātrīśikā 24); also the heart-centre of meditation (VBT 49).

The heart: seat of the self and of the space within it (ChU 3.14.3, 8.1.1-3); analysed as 'hṛdi ayam', 'this is in the heart' (ChU 8.3.3) and as hṛ-da-yam (BAU 5.3.1); where the knots and desires dwell (KU 2.3.14-15).
The Heart-mantra of Bhairava taught in the Parātrīśikā (identified by the commentators as SAUḤ), in which the universe lies in seed form.

The knot(s) of the heart: when they are cut the mortal becomes immortal (KU 2.3.15); when he is seen the knot is cut (MuU 2.2.8); the knot of ignorance (MuU 2.1.10); knots loosened by firm memory (ChU 7.26.2).
The knot of the heart: the ego-knot binding consciousness and the insentient, cut by knowledge (MU 2.2.8).
The Goddess's seed-syllable hrīṃ ('heart-letter'), placed in the body in daily worship.
A mark and special quality of the self (NS 1.1.10); 'desire is wanting' (Tarkasaṅgraha); eternal in the Lord.
The power of will, first of the three powers; in the Trika the goddess Parā; the Śiva Sūtra calls it Umā, the virgin (1.13).
The left channel, carrying the moon.
The third daily period: worship of Bhagavān.
The warrior king of the gods, soma-drinker, slayer of Vṛtra who released the waters (RV 1.32); some doubted him, and he answered 'here I am' (8.100.3–4).

notes: Scholarly metadata only (not used in interpretation): an Indra appears among the demons of the Avesta.

definitions.definition: 'Indra's birthplace': the passage between the palates, where the hair parts, by which the person made of mind goes out (TU 1.6.1).
The eleven capacities produced from ahaṃkāra: five sense capacities, five action capacities and manas (SK 24–27); not made of the elements (SS 2.20, 5.84).
Smell, taste, sight, touch, hearing, made from the elements (NS 1.1.12).
Each located in a bodily seat — nose-tip, tongue-tip, the black of the eye, the whole skin, the ear's ākāśa; manas is the inner sense.

The senses, which carry off the mind (BhG 2.60, 2.67), are withdrawn like a tortoise's limbs (2.58), and are high but lower than mind (3.42); in the Anugītā they are among the seven priests of the inner sacrifice (14.20).
The senses (ten, with manas eleven, YBh 2.19), part of the seen (2.18); withdrawn in pratyāhāra (2.54) and mastered by saṃyama on their five forms (3.47).
The eleven faculties — five of knowledge, five of action and mind — to be restrained like horses (MDh 2.88–92).
The doors of pleasure and pain, to be abandoned for abiding in the self (VBT 136); in the Śiva Sūtra, the spectators of the self's dance (3.11).
Supreme mastery of the senses from sense-withdrawal (2.55); also from saṃyama on their five forms (3.47); Vyāsa records several views of what it is (YBh 2.55).
Love and its joy; the Kuṟaḷ's third book (25 chapters), in the akam tradition of love poetry.
The two deeds, good (puṇṇiyam) and bad (pāvam), both binding the soul to birth — 'golden and iron fetters'.
In the Kuṟaḷ (v. 5) the two deeds 'born of darkness' do not cling to those who praise the Lord.

The 'equality of the two deeds': the state in which the soul's good and bad karma balance, so that it turns with equal indifference from both, a precondition, with the ripening of mala, of the descent of grace.

cross_language.note: the Sanskrit Āgamic term, with a debated sense

equivalents.note: Tamil usage stresses the soul's equanimity toward both deeds; the Sanskrit term the timing of śaktipāta

definitions.definition: Lord; the Vrātya 'became Īśāna' (AVŚ 15.1.5); a name of Rudra.
The Lord as 'Īśāna of all knowledges, lord of all beings', invoked in the fifth brahma-mantra that closes the Sūtra.
The deity with whom self-study brings contact (2.44); Vyāsa: gods, sages and perfected beings appear to the one devoted to self-study (YBh 2.44).

The gross liṅga given by the guru at initiation and worn outwardly on the body for life (SSM 6.49–50), worshipped on the palm (6.54–55) without invocation or dismissal because Śiva abides in it from the moment of initiation (10.44–47).

equivalents.note: both name the devotee's own chosen form of the divine; the iṣṭaliṅga is a physical sacrament worn on the body, which the iṣṭa-devatā need not be

literal: what is sacrificed and what is given

definitions.definition: The accumulated merit of sacrifices and gifts, with which the dead are reunited in the highest heaven (RV 10.14.8).
Sacrifices and works of merit (such as digging wells): those who venerate them win the moon and return (ChU 5.10.3; PrU 1.9); fools who think them best go to lower worlds (MuU 1.2.10).

literal: being a means to the desired

definitions.definition: Maṇḍana Miśra's account of what the injunctive form conveys: that the act is a means to what the agent desires.

notes: Assigned to lin:bhatta-mimamsa because Maṇḍana is placed there by tradition; the view differs from Kumārila's.

definitions.definition: The Lord dwelling in the heart of all beings, moving them by his māyā (BhG 18.61); the great Lord of beings who comes into being by his own māyā (4.6); in the Mokṣadharma, the Yoga thinkers' argument that without a Lord no one is freed (12.289.3).

Classical Sāṃkhya recognizes no established Īśvara as creator: Gauḍapāda argues the attributeless could not produce what has guṇas (on SK 61); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra holds 'Īśvara is not established' (1.92–99; 5.2–12; 6.64), yet admits emergent lords — the one absorbed in prakṛti who becomes all-knowing and all-doing (3.55–57). Theistic Sāṃkhya (Vijñānabhikṣu) salutes the Lord.

A special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25), teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by the praṇava (1.27); his lordship has no equal or superior (YBh 1.24).

A distinct self free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness, possessing merit, knowledge and concentration, who assists human effort and sets karma and the elements in motion; like a father to beings (NBh 4.1.21); the all-knowing maker of the world proved by inference (NK 5.1).
Maheśvara, by whose will the world is dissolved and created through the selves' adṛṣṭa (Praśastapāda).
The one omniscient supreme self with eternal cognition, desire and effort; author of the Veda; whose convention fixes word-meanings (Tarkasaṅgraha).
The Lord: Brahman associated with māyā (or reflected in it), omniscient ruler, creator, sustainer and dissolver, giver of the fruits of action; his lordship depends on adjuncts of name and form.
The prototype (bimba) consciousness, of which the jīva is the reflection.
Rejected as director of dharma and adharma and as creator: the fruit comes from dharma and adharma with place, time and circumstance (Prakaraṇapañcikā).
Kumārila rejects a creator Prajāpati (ŚV sambandhākṣepaparihāra 42–116); later Bhāṭṭas (Āpadeva, Laugākṣi Bhāskara) teach offering dharma to Īśvara/Govinda.
Nārāyaṇa, the third reality: the self of all, cause of the world, opposed to all evil and abode of infinite auspicious qualities, present in five forms.

The Lord: all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord (Īśa 1); the two birds, the Lord and the one who grieves (MuU 3.1.2); the great Lord of lords (ŚU 6.7); the māyin (ŚU 4.10); lord of all (BAU 4.4.22; MāU 6).

Devotion to Īśvara: a special bhakti by which Īśvara, won over, favours the yogin (YBh 1.23); offering all actions to the supreme teacher or renouncing their fruit (YBh 2.1, RM 2.1); a means to samādhi (1.23, 2.45), part of kriyā-yoga (2.1) and a niyama (2.32).
Fourth tattva: knowledge predominant; the outward 'unmeṣa' (ĪPK 3.1.3), 'this am I' with the 'this' prominent.
Performing dharma with the thought of offering it to Īśvara (Laugākṣi Bhāskara) or Śrī Govinda (Āpadeva), which makes it a cause of the highest good.
Traditional narrative (above all the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa), named with purāṇa as the fifth Veda.
The genre of the Mahābhārata, which calls itself a Veda of Kṛṣṇa (MBh 1.1.205).
The procedure — the subsidiaries (e.g. the prayājas) — that answers the question 'how?' of the bhāvanā; in an ectype it is taken from the archetype (MS 7.4.1).
The freed share all the Lord's powers except creating, sustaining and ruling the world (BS 4.4.17).
The world as Brahman's real, divine form, to be honoured, as opposed to saṃsāra.
The metre of four twelve-syllable lines.
A Vedic metre of 48 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
Waking: the field of the first quarter, vaiśvānara, outward-knowing, enjoying the gross (MāU 3).
Waking: the state in which the self, as viśva, experiences gross objects through the senses; empirically real.
Waking is [external] cognition (Śiva Sūtra 1.8).
Waking-dream: the waking mind's fancies and misperceptions (two moons, silver in shell, mirage).

literal: implication that leaves and does not leave

definitions.definition: Exclusive-non-exclusive implication: dropping the incompatible part of each word's meaning and retaining the compatible part, as in 'this is that Devadatta'; applied to 'tat tvam asi'.
Exclusive implication, which abandons the direct meaning entirely (the village 'on the Gaṅgā' = on its bank); rejected for 'tat tvam asi'.
Rudra's healing remedy (RV 1.43.4, 2.33.7).
Debate with the features of vāda in which quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat are also used (NS 1.2.2); permitted to protect the ascertainment of truth (NS 4.2.50).
Debate aimed at victory, one of the three kinds of debate among the learned.
The central island-continent with Meru at its centre, divided into nine varṣas, Bhārata being the southern one.

(1) The living, moving devotee or body as Śiva's true temple, against the fixed (Basava's vacana); (2) the wandering Śivayogin teacher whose greatness is taught in the prasādi-sthala — to see him gives accomplishment, to worship him is a means of liberation (SSM 11.37–43); (3) the order of Liṅgāyata priests and monks.
A holy person who, carrying the Lord within, makes even the tīrthas holy.
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the prāṇaliṅgi stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
Repetition of the praṇava together with contemplation of Īśvara, making the mind one-pointed (1.28, YBh 1.28); self-study includes repetition of purifying formulas (YBh 2.1).
Repetition of a mantra; audible, whispered and mental japa are ten, a hundred and a thousand times better than ritual sacrifice (MDh 2.85–87).
Muttering of the five brahma-mantras (the 'five purifiers') and the Raudrī Gāyatrī; the last limb of the offering; mental for the Ratnaṭīkā.
Repeated contemplation of the supreme state; the self-arising sound is what is repeated (VBT 144-145); the liberated's conversation is japa (Śiva Sūtra 3.27).
Silent recitation, the best of sacrifices ('among sacrifices I am japa', BhG 10.25).
Recitation in which each pair is said forward, backward and forward (ab ba ab, bc cb bc …).

(1) In debate: a futile rejoinder based merely on similarity or dissimilarity (NS 1.2.18), of twenty-four kinds (NS 5.1.1). (2) The universal, 'that whose nature is to produce sameness' (NS 2.2.71), part of a word's meaning (NS 2.2.68).
The universal (synonym of sāmānya), e.g. substance-hood; genuine universals are limited by six impediments (Udayana).

The SSM tells the māheśvara to give up the dharmas of his jāti and family that oppose steadfastness in the liṅga (10.30–31), yet prescribes commensality with twice-born of one's own jāti on the path (9.29), and makes brāhmaṇa and outcaste alike for those in the contemplation of Śiva (14.19–20).
The vacanas reject caste among devotees: Basava calls himself the son in the house of the cobbler Mādāra Cennayya and asks to say of every devotee 'he is ours'.
Birth-group; the mixed classes arising from unions across the varṇas (anuloma, pratiloma) described in MDh 10.
The real universal; in MS 6.1.8 the class (human) as the eligible agent.

notes: Homonym: other units define jāti as birth or social class.

definitions.definition: Six conditions that disqualify a property from being a genuine universal (Udayana).
Kṛṣṇa's birthday when the dark eighth coincides with Rohiṇī at midnight; kept by fasting.
The third stage, aimed at conquering the senses (and constant union with the god), in a cave or empty house.
The inquiry into the means of destroying the three sufferings, prompted by being struck by them (SK 1).
Rites for renovating a temple or replacing a damaged image.
Renovation followed by re-consecration (punaḥpratiṣṭhā) under the tantri.

The living self: the 'living self' (jīva ātman) with which being enters the elements (ChU 6.3.2); life which does not die when the body dies (ChU 6.11.3); in ŚU 5.9 the jīva is a hundredth part of a hundredth of a hair's tip yet fit for infinity.

The individual self: Brahman appearing as limited, reflected or semblanced through the adjunct of the inner organ (and ignorance); agent, enjoyer and transmigrant only through adjuncts; in truth Brahman.
The reflection of Brahman in avidyā/the inner organ, real and identical with the prototype.
Brahman delimited by the inner organ; the locus of ignorance.

A part of the formless Śiva through connection with beginningless ignorance, in whom Śiva abides as fire in the sunstone (SSM 5.34–36); at the prāṇaliṅgi stage the breath is the jīva and the great liṅga brahman (12.21–24).

The living being: the Lord's higher nature has become the life-element (BhG 7.5), and an eternal portion of him becomes the jīva (15.7); the living self in the body whose existence Bhṛgu defends (MBh 12.175–185).
The jīva is Saṃkarṣaṇa, arising from Vāsudeva (Nārāyaṇīya 12.326.38).
The individual self: eternal, atomic, a knower by nature and possessing attributive consciousness, agent and enjoyer dependent on the Lord, essentially his servant (śeṣa); countless in number.
An eternal, sentient, dependent self, atomic, distinct from God and from every other soul, a reflection (pratibimba) of God, with an innate fitness that fixes its destiny.
The inner self born with the body that experiences pleasure and pain (MDh 12.13).
The world of the living to which the widow is bidden to rise (RV 10.18.8).
Liberation while living: in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha the seventh stage, in which one acts as custom requires, unimmersed in pleasure and pain, the mind 'dead' (manonāśa).
The liberated one, though in the body, is not in it; his functions are free of intention; the body lives on while its karma lasts.
The destruction of ignorance, the fruit of human birth and the state of liberation while living.

The state of one who, after perfect knowledge, remains embodied through the momentum of impressions like a potter's wheel (SK 67); the Sāṃkhya Sūtra names the 'one liberated while living' and grounds it in the need for liberated teachers (SS 3.78–84).
